title: A Shared ChatGPT Link Could Run Attacker Code in Your Session and Read Private Chats
raw_text: A malicious ChatGPT share link could run an attacker's code in the logged-in session of anyone who opened it, allowing them to read their private conversations, researchers at the security firm Parameter showed. The researchers reported the flaw through OpenAI's bug bounty program on October 18, and OpenAI fixed it eight days later and rated it P1, its most serious category.

title: What’s new in AI infrastructure and orchestration in October
raw_text: The Google Cloud AI Infrastructure team had another busy month in October, filled with new product launches and updates to power today’s AI and agentic workloads scalably and efficiently. We were also honored to share our progress with customers, partners, and the broader community at leading industry events, including NVIDIA GTC, PyTorch Conference, and AGNTCon + MCPCon. Let’s dive in! Product, technology, and tools updates New compute service: Agent Compute Engine is a purpose-built compute service providing high-performance, hardware-isolated microVM sandboxes alongside expanded agent governance capabilities like Agent Gateway and Agent Registry, all in the service of securing and scaling autonomous AI agents. Its primary benefits include rapid sub-second activation, extreme workload density through copy-on-write memory sharing, enterprise-grade security and identity management, and cross-cloud observability. AI Hypercomputer updates: At NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026 we announced updates to our agentic infrastructure, including to A5X instances powered by the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, Virgo Network scale-out fabric, and Managed Lustre storage. These co-engineered advancements provide enterprises with accelerated performance, enhanced sovereign AI controls, while advanced Confidential Computing capabilities help you train and deploy complex multi-step models securely and efficiently. GKE product update: CPU startup boost for GKE , in preview, uses Kubernetes In-place Pod Resize to dynamically elevate container CPU resources during initialization and scale them back down to steady-state levels without having to restart the containers. This feature removes startup throttling and accelerates cold starts by up to 2x for demanding workloads, helping to lower cloud infrastructure costs. GKE product update: The preview of the Wiz Runtime Sensor add-on for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) brings low-touch deployment, automated lifecycle management, enterprise credential security, and fleet-wide governance to Wiz's eBPF runtime threat detection for both Standard and Autopilot GKE clusters. Modernization tools: Together at last. Google Cloud Modernize brings Google Cloud’s migration and modernization tools, including Migration Center, Google Cloud VMware Engine, Google Cloud Mainframe Modernization and our new EKS-to-GKE Migration Agent, into a single portfolio. Enterprise teams now have purpose-built agentic capabilities across infrastructure assessment, platform modernization, and application modernization. Cloud Run product update: Temporal Serverless Workers on Cloud Run automatically scale worker pools based on Temporal task queue demands and scale down to zero when idle. This integration eliminates cluster management, lowers costs, using Temporal Worker Versioning to safely handle stateful, long-running workflows and AI agent workloads. New open-source product: llm-d 1.0 is an open-source, Kubernetes-native serving stack that turns a cluster of model servers into a coordinated serving pool, unifying distributed LLM inference across mixed Google Cloud TPU and GPU fleets. Co-founded by Google and partners, it provides production-ready benefits such as cache-aware routing, tiered KV cache offloading, and priority-based flow control to dramatically improve context reuse, reduce time-to-first-token latency, and efficiently scale multi-tenant agent workloads. New open-source product: Working with Meta, we open-sourced TorchTPU , a native PyTorch stack that integrates Google TPUs directly into the PyTorch ecosystem alongside GPUs and CPUs. Now developers can train, serve, and deploy models natively on TPUs using familiar frameworks like Hugging Face, vLLM, and TorchTitan. Google Distributed Cloud updates: Organizations that operate under strict sovereignty mandates would love to use AI to help them process data, but can’t send it to the cloud. The latest version of Google Distributed Cloud (GDC) air-gapped brings frontier AI models and multimodal enterprise search with Gemini into these isolated environments. In addition, GDC air-gapped supports NVIDIA HGX B300 systems based on the NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra architecture, and features enhanced networking and security capabilities. Edge inference product: Google open-sourced ML Drift , a cross-platform on-device GPU compute engine built for LiteRT that abstracts hardware complexities across OpenGL ES, OpenCL, Metal, and WebGPU. The framework delivers peak performance, enhanced 5D tensor support, and memory efficiency for both classical machine learning workloads and advanced generative AI models at the edge. Open-weight model support: Reflection's Beam is an open-weight, 501-parameter model released under an Apache 2.0 license designed specifically for frontier software engineering and long-horizon agentic tasks. We announced day 0 support and ready-to-run deployment recipes for service Beam on AI Hypercomputer and NVIDIA AI Infrastructure. Practitioner guides and how-tos AI network reference architectures: In Networking for AI inference model serving - GKE only and for all other backends , learn about reference architectures for AI inference model serving that provide centralized governance and private IP routing using Private Service Connect, Apigee API Management, and Model Armor. These architectures simplify multi-model scaling and prompt security across GKE, Cloud Run, and hybrid clouds. How-to guide: A Tale of TPU Observability on GKE: Part 2 - Dynamic Slicing Enhancements breaks down GKE's new Dynamic Slicing observability tools and metrics for next-generation v7 TPUs through an engaging, story-driven observability guide featuring Alex, a lead AI platform engineer. Explore the step-by-step diagnostic workflows with real-world examples and handy command-line snippets. Check out Part 1 here . Customer and partner updates AI21 achieves an 83% reduction in time-to-start for AI workloads with AI Hypercomputer : Frontier lab AI21 needed a new stack on which to train its Jamba family, and chose AI Hypercomputer configured with GKE on A3 and A3 Ultra instances. By doing so, AI21 says it cut high-priority job wait times from 72 hours to 12, and manual scheduling interventions from 20 per week to zero. Visko streams real-time world models on Google Cloud TPUs : Visko, an AI startup developing interactive world models, deployed an end-to-end live inference pipeline that combines video generation, super-resolution upscaling, and synchronized audio onto a single Cloud TPU slice . In this blog, the team discusses how it engineered the pipeline, the architectural optimizations it made, and practical lessons for other startups building ultra-low-latency generative AI. ZenteiQ scales physical AI inference 4x with GKE and llm-d : In order to pre-train models that understand physical laws, governing equations, and numerical solvers, Indian AI startup ZenteiQ designed and built a large-scale batch synthetic data-generation pipeline that runs across multiple model families and feeds verified datasets into training runs. GKE and GKE Inference Gateway gave ZenteiQ the inference-routing layer within its pipeline to scale aggregate inference throughput 4.07x and grow daily output from 1.47 billion to 5.97 billion generated tokens for every 1,000 accelerators. Palo Alto Networks modernizes cloud-delivered security service : Palo Alto has worked with Google Cloud since 2018 to deliver its Prisma Access security service, and it was time to update it. In order not to compromise its security guarantees, Palo Alto separated the platform into two independently scalable layers: an ingress layer that handles traffic routing and forwarding running on GKE, with Axion C4A instances; and a security layer that handles threat inspection, running on dedicated single-tenant VMs fronted by an Internal Load Balancer. Each layer can now scale, update, and operate independently. Oracle is the first hyperscaler to provide TPUs outside Google Cloud : By deploying Google TPUs, Oracle is broadening the range of AI chips available through its Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), and giving customers more options for running AI workloads. Google TPUs on OCI will be available in 2027. Research, reports and deep-dives New resource: As enterprise organizations shift from isolated AI experiments to production-scale systems, different departments — from engineering and finance to executive leadership — often speak different technical dialects; The Encyclopedia of AI Infrastructure bridges that communication gap by demystifying complex infrastructure jargon. Analyst report: We are thrilled to announce that Google was named a Leader in the inaugural 2026 IDC MarketScape for Agentic AI Platforms . Deep dive: A companion technical guide describing the architecture of Agent Compute Engine and how Google’s Gemini team needed both the isolation of a VM and the speed and density of a container to deliver personal agents for every Gemini user. September 2026 Product, technology, and tools updates Google Kubernetes Engine updates: The GKE team is all about improving the scalability of the platform, and in September, those improvements came in many shapes and sizes: New feature: Need an execution runtime with higher density for your agentic workloads? We engineered the new open-source GKE Agent Substrate to run millions of sandboxes with 10x higher density than standard container runtimes. Agent Substrate also delivers sub-500ms resume operations at over 500 suspend/resume activations per second with a native zero-trust kernel and network isolation. Product update: GKE now has scale-to-zero capabilities built-in. No need to configure complex components to scale your workloads down, thanks to the HPA with the Autoscaling Metric and support for KEP-2021, which do the job for you, out of the box. Read the blog to learn more. Product update: Further, the GKE HPA (with the above-mentioned Autoscaling Metric) now lets you scale up and down based on custom PromQL metrics, in addition to standard metrics, allowing you to trigger workloads according to conditions that are meaningful and unique to your business. Read more here . New feature: Yet another scalability feature is GKE Pod snapshots , which lets you save the running state of your workload, including CPU and GPU memory, and restore it on demand. According to internal tests, GKE Pod snapshots can reduce AI inference start-up by as much as 89%. Learn more here . New migration tool: Finally, if you’ve always wanted to migrate your container workloads from AWS EKS to GKE but feared a daunting, high-friction engineering endeavor, we’ve just launched GKE agentic migration , a purpose-built agent plugin that replaces brittle, ad-hoc prompting with an AI-assisted migration pipeline protected by deterministic guardrails. Designed as a compilation of agent skills and a local Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, it uses AI to translate complex AWS EKS IaC and Kubernetes manifests directly into GKE landing zones. Get started with the onboarding guide . Feature updates: Reinforcement learning (RL) and evaluation workloads are a beast: In a standard agentic RL loop, an LLM policy generates actions like code snippets on GPUs and executes them inside isolated CPU sandboxes to observe a reward signal. However, when scaling up this loop to support tens of thousands of parallel rollouts, infrastructure bottlenecks emerge, for instance idle accelerators, image cardinality, and a saturated control plane. To help, we developed GKE Agent Sandbox optimized for RL, plus an Agent Sandbox RL orchestration SDK and native integrations for popular RL gyms and harnesses. All are now generally available, and you can learn more here . Storage updates: AI trains and creates lots of data, and that data has to live somewhere — in block storage systems, file systems, object stores and databases. We announced enhancements to our storage portfolio to help this critical layer roll with the agentic punches: Product update: Filestore agent volumes offer high-performance, elastic, persistent file storage for agentic workloads. Thanks to its tight integration with GKE Agent Substrate and GKE Agent Sandbox, Filestore agent volumes automatically allocates and attaches a dedicated, isolated file workspace to GKE agent sandboxes in milliseconds. Request access to the preview here . New product: If you run generative AI and RAG data layers — think Milvus, Pinecone, Qdrant, Vespa, Redis, and in-memory context caching — you may want to take a look at the M4N family of VMs , now GA, which offers the highest per-core IOPS and throughput of leading hyperscalers. Paired with Google Cloud's custom Titanium offload architecture and paired with Hyperdisk Extreme , M4N instances deliver up to 25,000 MiB/s (25 GiB/s) of aggregate host storage performance and up to 1 million IOPS. New product: Another new Compute Engine product, Z4D, is GA , and a strong storage solution for AI/ML training and inference workloads. When configured as a bare metal instance, Z4D provides both the high local SSD (LSSD) capacity and low latency required by agentic microVMs, so you can run thousands of isolated sandboxes per host with native performance and efficiency. Learn about Z4D machines here . Product update: Today’s AI training and inference pipelines create data faster than most storage management systems can keep up, creating challenges for teams trying to understand their storage estates. A new version of Storage Intelligence advisor makes it easier to answer the question: "What’s in my buckets?" and quickly identify unexpected changes. Then, enhanced batch operations let you automate bulk changes across your buckets — say, move storage classes, mass-delete stale or temporary data, or apply metadata, tagging, retention, or encryption changes. Learn about the latest in Storage Intelligence advisor here . New product: Last but not least, a new version of AlloyDB for PostgreSQL brings together pioneering Google infrastructure — Colossus distributed file system, and Jupiter network — to power a new, no-compromises database architecture for the agentic era . Practitioner guides and how-tos How-to: Wish you could make GPUs and TPUs scattered around the globe behave as a single pool behind a single entry point? In this blog , we show you how to do just that. At the edge, the multi-cluster GKE Inference Gateway focuses on global, multi-region traffic distribution and high availability. Beneath that, the LLM-d router handles complex, memory-aware scheduling algorithms to keep utilization high. This architecture is deliberately runtime-, model-, and accelerator-agnostic, and in tests, routing traffic through the multi-cluster GKE Inference Gateway added less than 1% overhead. Guide: Using or planning to use GKE on TPUs for AI model training or inference? Training massive Large Language Models (LLMs) or running high-throughput inference serving represents a significant investment in specialized AI hardware, such as Cloud TPUs and GPUs. To get the most out of every dollar spent, you need to understand workload lifecycle metrics in GKE . This detailed guide explains how to turn opaque cluster behaviors into actionable telemetry. Customer and partner updates GKE customer: Learn why gaming startup SeaVerse relies on GKE Agent Sandbox for its multi-tenant workloads , and how the platform helped it decrease its infrastructure costs by 60%. Research, reports and deep-dives In case you missed it, we’re also thrilled to share that Google has been named a leader, including achieving the highest score on either product or strategy, in three key analyst reports from Gartner and Forrester. Google is a leader in The Forrester Wave™: Public Cloud Platforms, Q3 2026 : Highest overall score of any cloud provider! Google named a Leader in 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Strategic Cloud Platform Services : Positioned furthest for “Completeness of Vision” of all vendors evaluated. Google is a Leader in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Container Management : Positioned highest in “Ability to Execute” of all vendors evaluated. Google Cloud achieved a Gold rating in the latest SemiAnalysis ClusterMax 3.0 report, which evaluates the reliability, performance, support, pricing, and security of GPU providers globally. See the full report for more . August 2026 Product, technology, and tools updates Product update: Filestore , Google Cloud’s first-party, secure, scalable NFS file service, has emerged as a popular storage platform for AI and agentic workflows, and now, it’s even better suited to the task, with a new backend storage layer built directly on Colossus , Google’s foundational distributed storage system. This new backend lets you provision IOPS independently from storage capacity, and is deeply integrated with GKE. In AI environments, this can help you service so-called agentic swarms — large groups of agents that need to read and write to a common dataset — without a drop off in performance. For more, check out the blog post . New feature: gVisor sandboxes are now available in distributed Ray clusters on GKE . In partnership with Anyscale, we introduced an experimental library for Ray that brings gVisor, Google’s open-source application kernel, directly into distributed Ray clusters. gVisor provides lightweight environments with stronger isolation than ordinary containers, plus fast startup times and low memory overhead. To try out these sandboxing capabilities on GKE, head over to the Ray sandboxing User Guide . Product update: Looking for high-performance, easy-to-use infrastructure on which to run a personal AI agent, but don’t want to spend a lot of money? New Cloud Run instances are dedicated, singleton compute runtimes on Cloud Run that won’t shut down when the agent is idle. Better yet, the cost to run a Cloud Run instance with 1 vCPU and 1 GiB of memory continuously for 30 days is just $5.70. Practitioner guides, documentation and how-tos How-to guide: Big news in Model Context Protocol (MCP) land: As of the 2026-07-28 specification, the protocol core is “completely stateless. The handshake is gone. The initialize / initialized handshake (SEP-2575) and the logical Mcp-Session-Id header (SEP-2567) have been removed entirely. Instead, every request is now self-describing and independent.” Whoa. Learn more about the changes that the latest MCP specification brings, and more importantly, how to implement them, in this Google Developers blog . Guide: Real-time AI systems make a mess of traditional network load balancing techniques. “Instead of handling isolated requests, the backend has to manage a continuous, live bidirectional stream. You’re dealing with a constant stream of audio chunks, transcripts, model outputs, and synthesized speech flowing back and forth simultaneously.” Things only get worse when the user gets involved. “The server has to immediately halt its current speech generation, pivot to update the context, maybe trigger a new tool, and start drafting a different response; this must be done without dropping the connection.” For a new approach to managing load in the AI era, read Scaling real-time AI agents with session-aware load balancing . How-to: Learn how to build an elastic, scalable LLM inference platform on GKE, even with a mix of different GPU accelerators. The proposed architecture combines Capacity Advisor and Compute Advisor, plus high-performance storage like RunAI:model streamer or GCPFuse with parallel downloads. Get all the details here . Documentation: The thing about hosts with GPUs or TPUs is that you can’t use live migration to update them, setting up a maintenance challenge. In this new docs page, learn how to update accelerator-equipped hosts according to your tolerance for downtime for your training and inference workloads. Documentation: Advanced Compute Images, or ACIs, are standardized image stacks for AI/ML and HPC infrastructure, so you don’t need to manually build your own custom images. In this new docs page, learn how to create an ACI image using the Google Cloud CLI, console, or SchedMD's Slurm workload manager . Guide: AI workloads are notoriously difficult to architect, resource-intensive, and bursty, which can also lead to scaling bottlenecks and large pools of underutilized — or misutilized — compute resources. A new blog outlines the three main ways to achieve dynamic capacity management in Google Cloud : 1) scheduling capacity for planned downtime; 2) maintaining automated fallback capacity for unplanned downtime; and 3) relying on GKE’s core orchestration capabilities to automate resource allocation. Customer and partner updates Business orchestration software provider UiPath was dealing with spiky workloads, and wanted more predictable costs. To get there, it re-architected its infrastructure, moving from isolated clusters to a shared Google Cloud GPU fleet that included both A3 VM instances (NVIDIA H100 GPUs) for training with G4 VM instances (NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs) for inference. You can read more about their architecture here . Mirendil , an frontier AI lab focused on accelerating AI development, announced that it is using AI Hypercomputer with both TPUs and NVIDIA GPUs to support its model pre-training and post-training applications. Replenit , a retail CRM provider, built its AI decision engine in Google Cloud, using BigQuery, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and open-source Gemma models that it runs on Cloud TPUs. This latter combination provided Replenit with 90% lower pipeline costs than their previous cloud provider, the company reports. Read the full case study for more. Malachyte architected its AI-powered e-commerce recommendation platform on top of Bigtable, Managed Service for Apache Kafka, Pub/Sub, Compute Engine, and last but not least, GKE. See how it all comes together in this blog . July 2026 Product, technology, and tools updates Product update: Google Cloud Managed Lustre is now GA, and available in four distinct performance tiers that deliver throughput ranging from 125 MB/s, 250 MB/s, 500 MB/s, to 1000 MB/s per TiB of capacity — with the ability to scale up to 8 PB of storage capacity. The Managed Lustre solution is powered by DDN’s EXAScaler, combining DDN's decades of leadership in high-performance storage with Google Cloud's expertise in cloud infrastructure. Product update: C4N network and storage optimized VMs are now GA . C4N is our first network- and block-storage-optimized VM series built to eliminate data-transfer bottlenecks. Powered by 5th Gen Intel Xeon Scalable processors and built on Google's Titanium offloading hardware, it achieves 400 Gbps network bandwidth, 95 million packets per second (MPPS), and up to 25 GiB/s of block storage throughput when paired with Hyperdisk Extreme. New feature: GKE Dataplane V2 up to 15K Nodes with Network Policies (GA) . This capability enables standard GKE clusters to scale up to 15,000 nodes while maintaining full active Network Policy enforcement, supporting the massive infrastructure needs of large enterprise and AI/ML customers. New feature: Co-operative time-slicing in llm-d . If you’re running reinforcement learning (RL) workloads, you can now interleave independent RL jobs onto shared physical hardware, increasing aggregate accelerator duty cycles from a ~40% baseline up to 70% without impacting model convergence or accuracy. New AI security tool: Looking to secure your AI supply chain on GKE , deploy AI workloads safely, and cut down on shadow AI? We open-sourced k8s-aibom, a lightweight, unprivileged Kubernetes controller that continuously monitors container clusters to automatically detect running AI runtimes (like vLLM and Triton) and generate standard CycloneDX Machine Learning Bill of Materials (ML-BOMs). Check out the k8s-aibom project and get involved. Practitioner guides and how-tos How-to guide: On July 27, Google announced Day 0 support for Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight model, the day weights were released. Whichever your preferred deployment path — via Model Garden, custom orchestration, or GKE with llm-d recipes — this guide offers detailed step-by-step instructions to help you evaluate and pilot Kimi K3 in Google Cloud. How-to guide: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) managed DRANET supports both GPUs and TPUs . There are several configurations to use this implementation, including standard cluster (where you have full control) and autopilot cluster (where Google does the heavy configs for you). Take a deeper dive in the hands-on lab, GKE Autopilot clusters with TPUs, GKE managed DRANET and Gemma 4 . How-to guide: Learn to run Ray on TPUs, not GPUs. In Part 1 of this two-part series, we discuss TPU slices (hint: Ray thinks of them as just another accelerator on which to schedule), then walk through Ray’s various AI libraries ( Part 2 ). How-to guide: Evaluate TPUs for sample workloads using a new microbenchmark suite that helps you accurately assess whether a device is achieving its theoretical performance specifications, and to identify specific performance gaps or architecture-specific bottlenecks. Dive in here . How-to guide: Scale your agents without killing your budget. Learn how GKE orchestration can help you safely pack more agents onto a fixed compute footprint with GKE Agent Sandbox and Pod snapshots. Whether your goal is performance or cost optimization, we teach you how to turn the right dials for optimal agent efficiency. Technical blueprint: Inside the optimization of Mistral 3 large inference on Ironwood. This blog outlines how one Google team optimized Mistral 3 large MoE model inference on Google’s Ironwood (TPU v7x), achieving a 1.5x performance gain. They did so with hybrid sharding, replacing linear VPU summations with tree reductions, optimizing GMM/MLA kernels, and adopting asynchronous scheduling. As a result, they boosted throughput by up to 48% while maintaining benchmark accuracy neutrality. Read the full blog here . Research, reports and deep-dives Report: Google was named a Leader in the inaugural Gartner Ⓡ Magic Quadrant™ for AI Infrastructure , positioned highest for ‘Ability to Execute’ and furthest for ‘Completeness of Vision’. Gartner called out Google’s proprietary scalable compute, integrated AI Hypercomputer architecture, and the scale of our AI compute capacity as key strengths. Download a copy here . Report: We recently surveyed more than 1,400 senior IT leaders for our State of AI Infrastructure report , and a resounding pattern emerged: The gap between AI ambition and infrastructure reality is widening. In fact, 83% of organizations say they require infrastructure upgrades to support production-grade agentic AI. Read the accompanying blog to understand how adapting your infrastructure to meet the demands that agentic applications place on your systems will help you move from pilot to production. June 2026 Product, technology and tool updates Product update: Protecting sensitive data used with AI is a critical part of advanced and secure cloud infrastructure. Confidential Computing cryptographically protects data in use in hardware-based Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) with verifiable data integrity, and is now available on the accelerator-optimized G4 machine series , featuring NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs . Get started with Confidential G4 VMs and Confidential G4 GKE Nodes . Developer resource: The new TPU Developer Hub is the place to go for model builders, optimizers, and developers to learn to unlock the full performance of Google Cloud TPUs. Read more in this blog . New product: Scale your AI workloads with the new OpenTelemetry-Based TPU AI Telemetry Collector Agent . For the first time, you can route high-fidelity TPU hardware telemetry to Google Cloud Monitoring, Google Managed Prometheus, or your own self-hosted Grafana stack. Practitioner guides and how-tos How-to guide: Learn how to build high availability into an AI inference workload running on GKE Inference Gateway with TPUs, Cloud Storage FUSE and Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA). This blog provides an overview, or you can get all the technical details in the hands-on codelab . How-to guide: Did you know you can connect your AI agents to unstructured data in Cloud Storage via Model Context Protocol (MCP)? In this blog , learn about why would want to do that from three customer examples, then how to do it, choosing either a fully managed service, or a self-managed local server for more customization and control. Research, reports and deep-dives Report: According to an independent benchmark report, GKE Inference Gateway outperforms the next leading managed Kubernetes service with 15.7% higher throughput, 92.8% shorter wait times, and 62.6% lower inter-token latency. This performance can be attributed to its use of prefix caching, which optimizes LLM performance by storing the KV cache (activation states) of long, repetitive prompt prefixes. Learn more in the blog . Architecture deep dive: A closer look at the cold start problem, this time for TPUs and GKE , and how the Run:ai Model Streamer can help change the dynamic. Customer and partner updates Customer win: Leveraging GKE, BigQuery, Cloud SQL, and Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Pager Health is eliminating operational fragmentation to deliver a simplified, personalized U.S. healthcare experience that transforms lives. Customer win: Trustpilot, the customer review platform, built a high-volume streaming pipeline using fine-tuned Gemma models with Dataflow and Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform running on cost-optimized A2 VMs using A100 GPUs, as well as optimized version of vLLM maintained by Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. May 2026 Product, technology and tool updates Product update: GKE Agent Sandbox is now generally available. New open-source project: Agent Substrate is a new open-source project aimed at continuing to push the limits of agentic infrastructure density New feature: Google AI Edge Portal , a solution for testing and benchmarking on-device machine learning (ML) at scale, now supports benchmarking and debugging on-device LLMs. Read more here . Product deep dive: We went into depth about Cloud Storage Rapid , a new family of high-performance storage offerings for AI workloads. At launch, offerings include Rapid Bucket (formerly Rapid Storage), a high-performance zonal object storage offering, and Rapid Cache (formerly Anywhere Cache), which accelerates reads on-demand and colocates compute and data for workloads in existing buckets. Research, reports and deep dives Architecture deep dive: Google Global Infrastructure VP Bikash Koley and Engineering Fellow Arjun Singh provide a high-level overview of the challenges that AI workloads pose to network infrastructure , and discuss the deep enhancements we’ve made to our data center fabrics, WAN, and global networks to better support them. Architecture deep dive: We unveiled a new cluster-level reliability model for developing frontier AI models on TPUs, ditching instance-level reliability Customer and partner updates Customer win: Visual media provider Imgix serves more than 8 billion images and videos from AI Hypercomputer equipped with G4 VMs powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs.

title: When the Kubernetes API went silent: A three-layer networking mystery
raw_text:
Every support engineer has a case that stays with them. The one that comes up at team lunches. The one where, even after it's resolved, you find yourself staring at a packet capture at midnight just to make sure you really understand what happened. This is that case. It started in January 2026 with a support ticket that read deceptively simply: pods are intermittently failing to reach the Kubernetes API server. The error was a familiar-looking timeout. The customer had already ruled out their own operators. What none of us knew yet was that we were looking at three separate bugs — in three different layers of the stack — all conspiring to produce the same symptom at the same time. By the time it was over, around 800 developers had been blocked from deploying to production for weeks on end, and GKE clusters across europe-west had ground to a halt. In a race to fix the problem, we involved engineers across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, networking, hostnet, kernel, and the Linux upstream community, who together tracked down not one but three distinct root causes. And the final fix landed not as a config change or a feature flag, but as a patch to the Linux kernel itself. This is the story of how we got there. Part one: The alarm bell that wouldn't stop The customer ran a large multi-cluster GKE environment in Google Cloud's europe-west region. Their clusters used Private Service Connect — Google Cloud's mechanism for exposing the GKE control plane privately — and had a rich ecosystem of system-level workloads: Twistlock security scanners, External Secrets Operator for secrets management, Cilium for network policy, as well as several internal Kubernetes operators. The first errors appeared in one of its user acceptance testing (UAT) clusters in europe-west, and a few days later in a second cluster in the same region. They looked like this: Application logs — pods across multiple namespaces code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "TimeoutError: Connect call failed ('1.2.3.4', 443)
dial tcp 1.2.3.4:443: i/o timeout

# 1.2.3.4 is the cluster's internal VIP for the kube-apiserver,
# routed through Private Service Connect"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd8f4121610>)])]> Initially the errors were intermittent — spikes in the logs, not a hard outage. The customer suspected their own code. Their team had recently deployed a custom operator built with the kopf framework, and it was the first thing they looked at. But the logs showed the errors had started eight days before the operator was ever deployed. When they shut it down completely, the timeouts kept coming. The issue persists even after completely scaling down the External Secrets Operator. The errors are appearing from customer workloads, and system-level pods we haven't touched. The growing list of suspects When a case like this arrives, the first instinct is to ask: what changed? The customer's timeline gave us several candidates, and we worked through them methodically. The custom operator (kopf): Ruled out immediately — errors predated deployment by a week and continued after shutdown. External Secrets Operator: Removed entirely on customer request. Timeouts continued in customer workloads that relied on Kubernetes control plane (KCP) connectivity, and cluster-internal system pods. Security agents: Uninstalled. Same result. We were now watching system-level Kubernetes components fail to reach their own control plane. conntrack table exhaustion: One theory was that too many half-open connections were filling the OS connection tracking table on the control plane nodes. We checked. The conntrack table was at roughly 50% capacity — of a default maximum of 1.3M entries. Not even close to exhaustion. Control plane overload: We scaled up the KCP VM size. kube-apiserver latencies looked healthy. No improvement on the timeout side. What made this case genuinely strange was the scope. We confirmed the timeouts were happening across five different clusters, affecting DaemonSets, Deployments, and system pods alike. External clients — developer laptops, GitHub Actions runners — were also hitting the same wall. This was not a broken workload. This was something wrong with the path between everything and the API server. The timeline so far Day 1: First I/O timeout errors appear (One of the UAT clusters in europe-west3. Intermittent, easy to dismiss.) Day 10: Errors become persistent (Frequency increases significantly. The issue is no longer dismissible.) Day 15: Case escalated — P0 bug filed (Multiple clusters confirmed affected. ~800 developers blocked. Production releases are frozen. Formal escalation begins.) Day 20: All obvious suspects ruled out (Custom operator, security agents, conntrack exhaustion, control plane resizing — all cleared.) Day 22: Packet captures collected (Captures taken simultaneously at the control-plane node NIC and from inside the kube-api container. The investigation enters its most critical phase.) With the obvious suspects cleared, and the scope undeniably wide, we did what you do when the application layer has nothing left to say: We went to the packets. Part two: Tracing the ghost in the wire To understand what the packet captures revealed, you first need to understand the architecture that a GKE pod traverses when it makes an API call. In a Private Service Connect-based GKE cluster, the path is deceptively long for something that looks like a local connection. (Note for formatting: Consider including the Pod → kube-apiserver flow diagram here: Pod -> Worker Node -> PSC NAT+Proxy -> ILB -> KCP VM NIC -> kube-apiserver) The key component here is Private Service Connect. When a pod dials 1.2.3.4:443 , it is not actually going directly to the control plane; that IP is a virtual endpoint. The connection is intercepted by Google's networking fabric, NAT'd through a Private Service Connect endpoint, passed through an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer, and ultimately delivered to the KCP VM, where Envoy acts as a local proxy in front of the actual kube-apiserver process. Private Service Connect adds a proxy protocol header to each new connection, so the kube-apiserver can see the real client IP. This will turn out to be important later. What the packets revealed When we captured simultaneously at the KCP VM's NIC (the PIGv interface, Google's programmable virtual NIC) and from inside the kube-apiserver container, we saw something striking. SYN packets from the pods were arriving at the KCP VM's NIC. They were getting that far. But instead of receiving a SYN-ACK in response — the expected second step of a TCP handshake — the client was getting back an out-of-place ACK. Not an RST. Not silence. An ACK that logically belonged to a different, earlier connection. Wireshark, the network protocol analyzer, was flagging these streams with a label that initially seemed innocuous: "TCP Port numbers reused." Wireshark — packet stream showing the failed handshake code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Time Source Port → Destination Port Info
09:13:41 10.0.13.77 53426 → 10.117.0.2 443 [SYN] Seq=0 Win=42600
09:13:41 10.117.0.2 443 → 10.0.13.77 53426 [SYN, ACK] Seq=0 Ack=1 Win=64768
 ... (data exchange, connection completes)
09:13:42 10.117.0.2 443 → 10.0.13.77 53426 [TCP Retransmission]
09:13:42 10.117.0.2 443 → 10.0.13.77 53426 [TCP Retransmission]
 ... (many retransmissions of the same ACK)

# 2 minutes later, same port 53426 is reused for a new connection
09:13:44 10.0.13.77 53426 → 10.117.0.2 443 [SYN] Seq=1498 ← NEW connection
 (expected: SYN-ACK)
 (received: ACK Seq=1498 Ack=1025 — belongs to PREVIOUS stream)
09:13:44 10.0.13.77 53426 → 10.117.0.2 443 [SYN] Retransmit...
09:13:44 10.0.13.77 53426 → 10.117.0.2 443 [SYN] Retransmit...
 → eventually: i/o timeout'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd8f41209d0>)])]> The pattern was clear. Something was causing the KCP VM to respond to a fresh SYN with an ACK that belonged to a different connection that had ended minutes ago . The old connection had used the same source port (53426 in the example above), and the KCP VM had never fully let go of it. "The KCP server sends FIN,ACK; client responds with FIN,ACK and then ACK. But KCP receives ACK before FIN,ACK. KCP server never ACKs the FIN,ACK — continuous retransmission of ACK. RST does not clear state." The "Invalid ACK" spike While one thread of the investigation was analyzing packet captures, a.k.a., pcaps, another team was digging into internal metrics for the Private Service Connect infrastructure — specifically the user space packet switch (USPS), Google's software switching layer that handles NAT and proxy protocol header injection for Private Service Connect connections. They found something alarming in the metrics for Andromeda, Google's networking fabric. A counter called "Proxy protocol drop: invalid ACK packet" had been flat for months — and then, in February 2026, it spiked sharply upward to several drops per second across the affected europe-west regions. That date matched a USPS version rollout. This version included a change which was a fix for a different bug but something about it had changed the behavior of how Private Service Connect handled a specific class of packet. Challenge ACKs: The RFC 5961 mechanism To understand the next piece of the puzzle, we need to talk about a TCP security mechanism called the challenge ACK, defined in RFC 5961. Imagine a TCP connection has closed — gone through the FIN/ACK dance and terminated. The server-side (here, the KCP VM) may still briefly remember the connection's sequence numbers in its TCP state machine. Now imagine that shortly afterward, a new client connection arrives on the same source port and destination port (the same 5-tuple). From the kernel's perspective, this could be a stale packet from the old connection, or it could be an attacker trying to inject data into what the kernel thinks is still an open session. RFC 5961 says: when you receive a SYN that matches an existing or recently-closed connection's remembered state, don't accept it blindly. Send a challenge ACK — an acknowledgment that carries the last known sequence number of the old connection. If the new client is legitimate, it will see this unexpected ACK, recognize the connection is stale, and send a RST to clear the state. The server then accepts the next SYN normally. The challenge ACK flow — how it's supposed to work code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# Step 1: New client sends SYN on a reused port
Client → Server: SYN (seq=X, same 5-tuple as an old connection)

# Step 2: Server is in FIN_WAIT_2, sends challenge ACK
Server → Client: ACK (ack=old_seq — "is this really you?")

# Step 3: Client recognizes the stale state, resets it
Client → Server: RST

# Step 4: State is cleared. Server accepts the next SYN normally.
Client → Server: SYN (new connection)
Server → Client: SYN-ACK ← handshake succeeds'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd8f4122350>)])]> This mechanism works perfectly — when the challenge ACK is allowed through . But that was exactly what the new USPS change was blocking. The culprit: A well-intentioned fix The change in USPS had been designed to fix a legitimate security issue in Private Service Connect's proxy protocol handling. Part of its effect was to drop packets it classified as "invalid ACKs" during the connection handshake phase — specifically, ACKs that arrived before the initial SYN-ACK had been sent, which in normal circumstances would be anomalous. Unfortunately, challenge ACKs look exactly like this: They arrive from the server before the new handshake has completed, in response to a SYN. From the USPS's new perspective, they looked like invalid packets. They were dropped silently. Why this broke GKE specifically: Private Service Connect uses NAT to share a single public endpoint across many client pods. This means many different pods — running on different nodes, from different namespaces — can all end up using the same source port after NAT, creating a high rate of 5-tuple collisions. The challenge ACK mechanism was being triggered far more often than it would be in a normal direct-connection scenario. The USPS fix hadn't introduced challenge ACKs — they had always been there. It had introduced the dropping of them, which broke a flow that GKE's TCP stack had silently depended on to clear stale state. Mitigation: Rolling back the change In February, we rolled back the USPS change , restoring the old behavior where challenge ACKs were passed through instead of dropped. The rate of "Proxy protocol drop: invalid ACK packet" dropped back toward baseline almost immediately. By early March , 2026, the customer confirmed that all affected clusters had recovered. No more timeout errors. But the rollback wasn't a fix. It was a band-aid. It restored the behavior the system had accidentally depended on . The deeper question — why was the KCP VM in FIN_WAIT_2 for over two minutes in the first place? — was still completely unanswered. That question led to Part 3. And it's where things got genuinely strange. Part three: Three bugs, one crime scene The mitigation bought us time, but it left a question hanging in the air: Why did the KCP VM keep connections in FIN_WAIT_2 for so long? A well-behaved TCP stack processes a FIN, acknowledges it, and closes the connection. The KCP VM was failing to do this, leaving half-open connections that persisted for more than two minutes — long enough for the port to be reused by Private Service Connect's NAT layer, long enough to cause the challenge ACK scenario we'd uncovered. To answer this, we needed to understand not just one bug, but three distinct failure modes that had intersected at the worst possible moment. Bug #1: Packet reordering at the PIGv The first piece was discovered through careful analysis of simultaneous captures at two points: the KCP VM's host NIC (inside the physical host running the VM) versus the PIGv — the virtual NIC as seen by the VM. At the host NIC level, packets arrived in perfect order. But by the time they crossed through USPS and appeared at the PIGv, they had been subtly reordered. This happens because of how Private Service Connect's miss-thread processing works. When Private Service Connect intercepts a new flow it hasn't seen before (a "miss"), it processes that packet through a slower path that adds the proxy protocol header and sets up NAT state. Subsequent packets in the same flow take a fast path. The consequence: a FIN or RST packet belonging to a flow in mid-close might arrive slightly out of order relative to the ACKs that followed it. What the KCP VM actually received (reordered sequence) code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "# What should have happened:
Client → Server: FIN, ACK (client initiates close)
Server → Client: ACK (server acknowledges client FIN)
Server → Client: FIN, ACK (server initiates its own close)
Client → Server: ACK (client acknowledges server FIN)
 → Connection fully closed. Both sides free.

# What the KCP VM actually received (reordered by PIGv/USPS):
Client → Server: ACK (arrives first — out of order)
Client → Server: FIN, ACK (arrives second, but kernel sees ACK first)
Server → Client: FIN, ACK (server sends close, enters FIN_WAIT_1)
Client → Server: FIN, ACK (old, now-reordered FIN from client)
 → Server should ACK this. But it doesn't..."), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd8f4121890>)])]> The reordering put the client's FIN after the server had already sent its own FIN. The server entered FIN_WAIT_1, then FIN_WAIT_2 after seeing the client's ACK of the server's FIN. But then the client's own FIN arrived — and the server's kernel ignored it. Bug #2: Envoy's half-close and the frozen timer Why couldn't the operating system clean up on its own? There is a Linux kernel parameter called tcp_fin_timeout that governs exactly this: how long a socket in FIN_WAIT_2 waits before being forcibly closed. On the KCP VM, this was set to 60 seconds. But tcp_fin_timeout only applies to orphaned sockets — sockets that no process is currently holding open. Envoy, the proxy that sits in front of kube-apiserver on the KCP VM, was performing a half-close: it called shutdown(SHUT_WR) , which closes the write side of the connection but keeps the socket open so it can still receive data. This is perfectly valid TCP behavior and is how graceful half-duplex termination is supposed to work. The side effect: As long as Envoy held the socket with SHUT_WR , the kernel did not consider it orphaned. tcp_fin_timeout never started. The socket sat in FIN_WAIT_2 indefinitely, waiting for a client FIN it would never be able to process correctly. Kernel socket state — captured via netstat just before a new connection code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Proto Local Address Foreign Address State
tcp 10.128.0.5:443 10.0.13.77:53426 FIN_WAIT_2
# This socket has been in FIN_WAIT_2 for > 120 seconds.
# tcp_fin_timeout=60 has not fired because the socket is not orphaned.
# Envoy holds it open with SHUT_WR.

# 2 minutes later, Private Service Connect NAT reuses port 53426 for a new pod connection.
# The kernel sees the new SYN on this 5-tuple and sends a challenge ACK.
# USPS drops the challenge ACK. → i/o timeout.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd8f4120490>)])]> Bug #3: The Linux kernel's silent failure But there was still a missing piece. Even with the reordered FIN, a healthy kernel should still process a received FIN in FIN_WAIT_2 and move to TIME_WAIT . The socket should eventually close. Why wasn't it? This led us deep into the Linux TCP state-machine implementation. When the reordered client FIN arrived at the KCP VM, the kernel's tcp_ack() function was called to process it. And here, in kernel version 6.1 (which underpinned the Container-Optimized OS (COS) running on the KCP VMs), there was a bug. RFC 5961 added stricter validation for acceptable ACK numbers — specifically, an ACK could be considered valid even if it was slightly "old" (within a sequence number window), to handle network reordering. But in kernel 6.1, there was a code path where tcp_ack() returned zero — indicating "this packet was not fully processed" — when it encountered an ACK that was old but within the RFC 5961 acceptable window. The caller of tcp_ack() in the FIN processing path checked this return value, saw zero, and did… nothing. The FIN was received and silently discarded. The Linux kernel commit that fixed it (upstream) code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'commit 795a7dfbc3d9
Author: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
net: tcp: accept old ack during closing

tcp_ack() returns 0 when ack is old but acceptable wrt rfc5961.
In FIN_WAIT_2, this caused tcp_fin() to never be called for a
valid received FIN, leaving the connection stuck indefinitely.

Fixed: properly handle old-but-acceptable ACKs during connection close.
Introduced in 6.1, fixed in 6.9.7. LTS backports: 6.6.y and 6.1.y.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd8f41225d0>)])]> The bug had existed since kernel 6.1 and was already fixed in kernel 6.9.7 — but GKE's KCP VMs were running COS builds based on 6.1 and 6.6. The fix needed to be backported and shipped as a COS image update. How the three bugs combined Individually, none of these three issues would have caused an outage of this magnitude. It took all three acting together to create the failure: Bug #1 alone: Packet reordering is mildly disruptive, but the kernel would normally still eventually process the FIN and clean up, just slower than ideal. Bug #2 alone: Envoy's half-close is perfectly correct behavior. It only becomes a problem if the FIN is never properly processed. Bug #3 alone: The kernel's failure to process old-but-acceptable ACKs would cause some connections to linger, but the impact would be limited without the port-reuse pressure from Private Service Connect NAT. All three together: Reordering causes the FIN to arrive out of sequence; the kernel bug prevents it from being processed; Envoy's SHUT_WR prevents the timeout from firing; the socket stays in FIN_WAIT_2 indefinitely. Private Service Connect NAT reuses the port. challenge ACK is sent. The USPS fix drops it. Connection fails. The resolution: A three-pronged fix Resolving this required action at three different levels, coordinated across multiple teams over several weeks: Immediate mitigation (Feb, 2026): Rollback of change in USPS. Restored the previous behavior where challenge ACKs were forwarded rather than dropped. Customer clusters recovered by early March. Correctness fix: A replacement change to handle the challenge ACK scenario properly in the Private Service Connect proxy protocol layer, rather than simply restoring the old drop behavior. A PacketDrill test was added to the test suite to prevent regression. Root cause fix — Linux kernel patch: Upstream patch ("net: tcp: accept old ack during closing"), authored by Eric Dumazet. Merged into Linux 6.9.7. Backported to 6.6.y and 6.1.y LTS branches. — shipping in GKE 1.33.5 and later. The bug is fully resolved at the OS level for all GKE versions running these COS images. What made this case different Most networking cases resolve at one layer. You find the misconfigured firewall rule, the exhausted connection pool, the miscalculated MTU. You fix it and move on. This one was different because the symptom — i/o timeout on a connection that never completed — was the same whether you were looking at the Private Service Connect layer, the kernel's TCP state machine, or Envoy's connection management. Every layer had a plausible explanation, and every explanation was incomplete. What finally cracked it was the discipline of simultaneous packet capture at multiple points in the path. Without captures at the host NIC, the PIGv, and inside the container at the same time, we would never have seen the reordering. Without correlating those pcaps to the USPS metric spike on February 18, we would never have found the dropped challenge ACKs. And without reproducing the issue in a lab environment, we would never have found the kernel bug that made the FIN_WAIT_2 state permanent. The other thing that made this work was the team. Over the course of two weeks, engineers from seven or eight different specialties contributed: GKE networking, Private Service Connect infrastructure, Hostnet, Andromeda, KCP, and ultimately the kernel community. No single person could have held all of this in their head. The case notes, the shared bug tracker, the meticulously collected pcaps — they were the connective tissue that let a distributed team work as one. In the end, the customer got back to production. The kernel got a better bug fix. And the rest of us got a very good story about why packet reordering, half-closed sockets, and a well-intentioned security patch should never be allowed in the same room at the same time. This blog is based on real case data from an anonymized customer support engagement and internal bugs. The Linux kernel fix referenced is commit 795a7dfbc3d9 , authored by Eric Dumazet. Special thanks to the engineers across GKE, Private Service Connect, Hostnet, Andromeda, COS, and the Linux networking community whose work made this resolution possible.
summary: Every support engineer has a case that stays with them. The one that comes up at team lunches. The one where, even after it's resolved, you find yourself staring at a packet capture at midnight just to make sure you really understand what happened. This is that case.

title: Innovate on your own business terms: Google Cloud spend caps now generally available
raw_text: Today, we’re announcing that spend caps on Google Cloud Budgets are generally available. With this release, we’re delivering ways to protect your workloads from runaway costs without risking resource deletion. More importantly, we’re introducing three major updates, directly inspired by your feedback since the initial preview, to bring programmability, real-time visibility, and automated guardrails to your cost-control playbook. How the new spend caps can help your business We have significantly enhanced the usability and power of spend caps in three ways: 1. Automation through spend caps API : Managing guardrails manually across hundreds of projects is a major operational challenge. To address this, we have launched the spend caps API, which can be accessed from the existing Cloud Billing Budgets API. You can now programmatically enforce your financial boundaries for eligible services within each project, without additional overhead. You can automatically lift, update, or delete caps on the fly and instantly apply a spend cap whenever a developer spins up a new sandbox project. 2. Real-time visibility with live cost reports: Spend caps for AI services trigger within minutes of usage using estimated, live costs. When a cap triggers, you need to know exactly why and when the limit was breached. You can now view these faster, estimated costs directly inside your Cost Reports. Instead of waiting hours for standard billing pipelines to settle net costs, you get the exact financial snapshots that triggered the enforcement, giving you the immediate context needed to run a precise root-cause analysis. 3. Automated guardrails for your monthly resets: Before, once a spend cap was triggered, the usage block remained locked until you manually lifted it in the UI. Today, we are introducing automated monthly resets. You no longer need to worry about manually lifting caps every month. Enforced spend caps will automatically reset, and blocked services will seamlessly resume at the beginning of the next month. However, if your governance policies require a strict manual audit before resuming operations, the manual override option continues to exist exactly as before. Best practices for deploying spend caps As you roll out spend caps across your organization, keep these operational tips in mind: Target non-production environments first : Start by applying strict, low-dollar spend caps to your developer sandboxes, testing clusters, and experimental AI agent playgrounds. Configure alerts wisely : Default alerts are automatically sent to billing administrators and project owners at 50%, 80%, and 100% of the cap. Make sure the right folks are set up in these roles. This ensures your team is never caught off guard when a budget is nearing depletion. Spend caps permissions can also be added to custom roles, if needed. Understand fixed vs on-demand costs : Spend caps halt pay-as-you-go and CUD-covered requests once the budget threshold is hit. However, Provisioned Throughput is never halted; requests using reserved capacity will continue to run, and serve traffic normally. Refresher on GCP’s dual-pronged defense playbook Spend Caps work seamlessly alongside our native Early Anomalies Detection to provide a closed-loop defense for your cloud spend. Read our previous blog for a detailed explanation on how to use these tools to effortlessly set up a GCP defense playbook. Playbook step Feature Focus Core action Key benefit Step 1 Early anomalies Predictive monitoring Analyzes early cost signals daily to alert you of directional spend variances Spot anomalous cost spikes early and pinpoint the exact SKU driving the trend Step 2 Spend caps Financial enforcement Programmatically pauses usage for a specific project/service once a budget is breached Absolute protection against runaway spend without deleting resources Get started today Spend caps are now ready to support your workloads at scale. Read our documentation for more details and navigate to the Budgets and Alerts page in your Google Cloud Billing Console, to set your first spend cap. To integrate programmatic guardrails into your deployment workflows, check out our newly published spend caps API documentation .

title: Querying Databricks Apache Iceberg Tables with the borderless Lakehouse
raw_text:
Enterprise organizations often leverage multiple data platforms, including Databricks, to execute heavy Apache Spark jobs alongside BigQuery to power highly concurrent analytics workloads. Historically, bridging these systems often meant building complex pipelines to copy data between environments. This approach increases storage costs, introduces latency, and fragments security controls. With Google Cloud’s borderless Lakehouse, you can now query Databricks-managed Apache Iceberg tables straight from BigQuery. This zero-copy approach removes the need to duplicate data: BigQuery reads the same files Databricks writes, and new changes appear after Lakehouse's next scheduled metadata refresh (as often as every 5 minutes). How Lakehouse and Databricks work together Managed Iceberg tables automatically generates Iceberg-compatible metadata alongside native Delta logs. Data engineering teams can store Parquet files once in Google Cloud Storage (GCS) using Databricks. Rather than loading this information into BigQuery, Lakehouse reads the Iceberg metadata directly, applying BigQuery’s vectorized engine directly to open-format files in GCS. Although Google Cloud Storage (GCS) serves as the primary storage layer in the above example, Lakehouse extends this borderless federation directly to external cloud environments like Amazon S3 and Azure Blob Storage. By pairing the open Apache Iceberg REST Catalog with cross-cloud connections, Lakehouse lets BigQuery query data across clouds without moving it. Each federated catalog lives in a Google Cloud location you choose, ideally the region closest to your data. This lets BigQuery read open-format Parquet files where they live, delivering multi-cloud analytics without replication pipelines. Remote-cloud egress charges still apply, but Cross-Cloud Interconnect (AWS) and Lakehouse caching can reduce them. Beyond simply querying external data, Lakehouse framework establishes true read and write (R/W) interoperability across engines. Because the platform is built on an open Apache Iceberg foundation, data teams can effortlessly execute multi-statement SQL commands directly inside BigQuery. Centralized security and governance Handling access controls across disparate systems can introduce vulnerabilities. Lakehouse addresses this through delegated access. Administrators can configure a BigQuery Cloud Resource Connection tied to a service account that manages IAM rights for GCS buckets. Granting users access to the Lakehouse table entity lets you enforce BigQuery controls including row-level, column-level security, and dynamic data masking on external Iceberg tables while Databricks handles ingestion. Catalog federation and credential vending Previously, connecting these platforms meant manually configuring BigQuery queries to point at static metadata paths. Modern setups leverage the open Apache Iceberg REST Catalog API. Databricks Unity Catalog functions as the central metadata layer, allowing a BigQuery administrator to establish a Lakehouse runtime catalog with a federated connection. When running a query, Lakehouse contacts Unity Catalog for current table state, and short-lived tokens are issued through credential vending to grant BigQuery temporary read access to GCS. Partition pruning BigQuery uses each table's Iceberg metadata to plan the query, then reads only the relevant data files in place. Iceberg's hidden partitioning lets you filter on logical columns, such as timestamps, without knowing the directory layout. Note that Databricks managed Iceberg tables don't support partition transforms; Databricks recommends liquid clustering instead. Filters in a standard WHERE clause let BigQuery use the Iceberg manifests to skip partitions that can't match. Compare partition columns with literal values so pruning can apply. These manifests maintain detailed column-level statistical bounds, enabling BigQuery to bypass irrelevant manifest records and unneeded Parquet files immediately. Consequently, queries scan only necessary byte ranges, accelerating query execution while significantly reducing on-demand slot consumption and storage scan costs. Fast queries with Iceberg metadata and Lakehouse caching Iceberg manifests already identify which data files to read, so BigQuery doesn't need a metadata cache for Iceberg tables. For cross-cloud tables, such as those in Amazon S3, Lakehouse caching (Preview) keeps retrieved data blocks in Google Cloud so repeat queries read them locally. BigQuery reads the Iceberg manifest files directly when it plans each query; there's no metadata caching to enable. This dynamic partition pruning bypasses unneeded files, significantly reducing runtime and bytes scanned. Maintenance and lifecycle management Modern lakehouses demand active upkeep; without routine care, performance degrades into an inefficient repository. Fortunately, both BigQuery and Databricks supply native capabilities to preserve table hygiene and accelerate analytical workloads. Keeping your tables optimized To maintain optimal query performance, active maintenance of your lakehouse storage footprint remains necessary. Trigger regular compaction pipelines via Databricks APIs to merge tiny Parquet files into larger, optimized layouts and use Predictive Optimization. Execute the Databricks VACUUM command to clear unreferenced files outside active snapshots, avoiding extra GCS storage costs. Compaction and the small file problem Frequent write operations, continuous ingestion jobs, and streaming workloads continuously produce thousands of small Parquet files. This fragmentation creates a storage bottleneck that can limit BigQuery’s reading efficiency. Establishing thousands of network connections to GCS and processing metadata footers across numerous tiny files consumes significant compute time, diminishing the performance advantages of vectorized query execution. Running routine compaction within Iceberg resolves these inefficiencies. Databricks manages this automatically using Liquid Clustering which dynamically adjusts file layouts based on access patterns or through native table management utilities. To compact small files manually on Databricks, run OPTIMIZE: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "-- Run on Databricks to compact small files
-- On Databricks:
OPTIMIZE customer_events;
-- For Iceberg tables you manage outside Databricks:
CALL my_catalog.system.rewrite_data_files(
table => 'default.customer_events',
strategy => 'binpack',
options => map(
'target-file-size-bytes',
'268435456',
'min-file-size-bytes',
'67108864'
)
);"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd8e72c69d0>)])]> Executing this command aggregates scattered file segments into larger, structured blocks typically between 256MB and 512MB that can help improve BigQuery’s scan throughput. The binpack approach operates rapidly by prioritizing total file size balancing, though alternative sorting strategies can organize dataset ordering along specific column keys. Managing orphan files and snapshot retention (VACUUM) Every transactional update, record modification, and table compaction creates fresh snapshots within Iceberg to preserve dataset integrity. Over time, historical Parquet objects detached from active table states become orphaned. Although these legacy files facilitate time-travel analytics, neglecting them can drive up GCS storage charges over time. Data teams can use the Databricks VACUUM operation to scan and purge abandoned storage files. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "ALTER TABLE customer_events SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration' = '7 days');
VACUUM customer_events FULL;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd8e72c68d0>)])]> Standard configurations apply a mandatory seven-day threshold (deletedFileRetentionDuration) before executing VACUUM routines. Preserving this delay prevents active analytical jobs from encountering missing file errors while keeping historical recovery options available. Scheduling routine VACUUM jobs, or letting predictive optimization run them, removes unreferenced data files and, for tables with Iceberg reads, old Iceberg metadata. That keeps storage costs low and performance high across your lakehouse. Conclusion Connecting Databricks Apache Iceberg datasets to Lakehouse can help you activate your data with BigQuery. By separating processing from underlying storage, embracing open formats, and using standard REST APIs with credential vending, you can run scalable engineering workloads and concurrent analytics without migrating data or sacrificing performance Pairing Databricks Iceberg reads (UniForm) with Lakehouse federation, Lakehouse caching, and regular OPTIMIZE and VACUUM maintenance helps you build an efficient, zero-copy lakehouse. This approach can help lower storage spend, avoids fragile pipeline maintenance, and prepares your data environment for modern analytics and emerging AI workloads. Constructing a unified architecture no longer requires moving data files across platforms. You can begin querying Databricks Iceberg tables by registering them with the Lakehouse runtime catalog today for bi-directional federation. Learn more by reading our documentation to get started.
