title: Cloud CISO Perspectives: Introducing new $250,000 tier for Google Cloud VRP (Q&A)
raw_text: Welcome to the second Cloud CISO Perspectives for October 2026. Today, Chris Betz talks with Michael Cote, our vulnerability rewards program lead, about the new tier of our Cloud VRP program and the current state of vulnerability rewards. As with all Cloud CISO Perspectives, the contents of this newsletter are posted to the Google Cloud blog . If you’re reading this on the website and you’d like to receive the email version, you can subscribe here . aside_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('title', 'Get vital board insights with Google Cloud'), ('body', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd8e7624450>), ('btn_text', 'Visit the hub'), ('href', 'https://cloud.google.com/solutions/security/board-of-directors?utm_source=cgc-site&utm_medium=et&utm_campaign=FY26-Q2-GLOBAL-GCP39634-email-dl-dgcsm-CISOP-NL-177159&utm_content=-&utm_term=-'), ('image', None)])]> Why we've created a new $250,000 tier for Google Cloud VRP (Q&A) By Chris Betz, CISO, Google Cloud The Google Cloud Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP) partners with the global security research community to help elevate cloud security for all by encouraging the discovery of critical software vulnerabilities. In an era when automated research has made it more challenging to verify authentic vulnerabilities, we have a critical need to boost high-level, human-led research that can transcend automated-only discovery. Today, we are expanding our top reward tier with a new $250,000 Root-in-Cloud reward , specifically designed to recognize high-impact architectural research. Identifying tenant-isolation bypasses and complex cross-service logic flaws requires human creativity, intuition, and rigorous systems analysis combined with the power of agentic systems. To earn this premier reward, you must demonstrate full administrative control, the equivalent of “roles/owner” or complete IAM control, over arbitrary Google Cloud organizations or projects with no prior access or special project setup. The exploit path can not depend on: Pre-existing access or footholds in the victim project. Leaked, phished, or stolen credentials. User interaction or social engineering. Proof-of-root: Clear, cryptographic validation To make testing safe, clear, and reproducible, without impacting production environments, we have defined technical criteria for validating root-in-cloud access . Additionally, valid vulnerability reports demonstrating remote code execution (RCE) in underlying Google production infrastructure (Borg) or achieving root-in-prod will automatically be evaluated by the Google Cloud VRP panel for root-in-cloud eligibility. Because code execution in Borg has the potential to impact service availability or cross-tenant data, researchers must halt all probing immediately upon achieving any execution in Borg. Escalation, extracting production credentials, and lateral movement are not allowed and will result in researcher disqualification. The Google Cloud VRP panel will analyze the initial entry point, execution context, and attack surface to determine whether full arbitrary tenant or project takeover is achievable from that position, and award the bounty accordingly. This new bounty tier reflects how security research continues to evolve, and the importance of continuing to recognize the most innovative and valuable security research. As part of those efforts, Google Security held its annual Escal8 conference in Singapore last week, and I had the opportunity to discuss the changing landscape with Michael Cote, Google Cloud’s vulnerability reward program lead. The following transcript has been lightly edited. Chris Betz : You are at Escal8 in Singapore announcing the new $250,000 Root-in-Cloud tier for our VRP. Why introduce this tier now, and what kind of research are you hoping to spark? Michael Cote : This is a recognition of how the field of security research has changed over the past year. We value quality submissions from anyone, and we’ve seen that the combination of human creativity and agentic power is much richer than either on its own. While automated scanners generate a high volume of low-impact noise, first-time researchers who pair human intuition with agentic tools are finding, on average, more interesting bugs than novices did two years ago. With the new Root-in-Cloud tier, we want to challenge the community and increasingly reward the complex, high-impact findings — like tenant-isolation bypasses and cross-service logic flaws — that require deep architectural intuition alongside agentic tools, because getting that information is essential to protecting our customers. Chris Betz : Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) recently shared research showing that monthly CVE disclosures have doubled as agentic tools mature. From your seat leading the Cloud VRP, how has automation technology impacted the reports we’ve received? Michael Cote : It has transformed our intake volume, though not in the way many people assume. While the number of valid vulnerability reports submitted to the Google Cloud VRP has remained stable over the last 18 months, the total number of reports has grown tremendously. Automation has helped democratize vulnerability discovery, and the barrier to entry has been rapidly flattening, something even our top researchers noted at Escal8. Because we’re seeing more researchers and more first-timers with interesting bugs, that creates pressure on more experienced researchers to move faster and bring more impactful findings — although their experience continues to be a key differentiator in success. Chris Betz : I’ve been working with the research community for more than 20 years. One of the things I appreciate most is how much the community values making the world more secure. Bounty programs let us recognize this valuable work. How do you see the community changing as we move further into the agentic era? Michael Cote : That shared commitment to making the world more secure is still the heart of this community, which is why the pressure to move faster is something we have to watch closely. As our GTIG colleagues found, the sharpest rise in the number of exploited vulnerabilities comes from n-days, not zero-days . Open source accounts have suggested that threat actors are using LLMs to rapidly turn newly-public vulnerability details into working exploits. When triage teams are already working through a surge in report volume, disclosing an unmitigated vulnerability well ahead of the standard 90-day coordinated disclosure window gives attackers the exact knowledge and time window they need to target customers. With the influx of new submissions, I worry about a growing pressure to rush to publish. Something that concerns me because we’re already seeing early indications of it. Because LLMs lower the barrier to finding bugs in source-available software, researchers worry that waiting to verify risks will allow someone else to be first to publish. Even more concerning, that same competitive pressure can tempt even established security companies to disclose unmitigated vulnerabilities without coordination, and that rush puts our users directly at risk. Project Zero helped establish the industry’s 90-plus-30-day responsible disclosure policy, and autonomous detection and exploitation capabilities make following coordinated disclosure more important than ever. In the long run, rushing to be first works against a security company's own self-interest. Novel discoveries may bring temporary visibility, but customers will ultimately choose not to work with organizations that put them and the broader ecosystem at risk. Chris Betz : When you offer a $250,000 bounty, how do you make sure researchers can validate their findings without putting customer environments or service availability at risk? Michael Cote : High incentives require clear, safe rules of engagement. We never want researchers testing exploits against real customer projects. Instead, we created a deterministic proof-of-root mechanism using a designated service account. Researchers can cryptographically prove unauthorized access against that identity. We’ve also updated our program rules to establish strict boundaries around underlying production infrastructure. If researchers think they are close to a breakthrough but are uncertain where the boundary lies, we encourage them to reach out. We are always more than happy to work with them to ensure they are recognized and rewarded for the value of their research without taking steps that would invalidate the bounty. Chris Betz : What should enterprise CISOs take away from these trends? Especially those who run their own vulnerability management pipelines and partner with external researchers, what advice would you offer for navigating this AI inflection point? Michael Cote : First, prepare your vulnerability triage workflows for agent-generated submissions. To keep valid reports from getting stuck in a backlog, security teams need ways to separate plausible-sounding hallucinations from real security risks. Second, compress your remediation timelines once a vulnerability becomes public. Defensive patching and mitigations have to move faster because autonomous technology compresses the time from disclosure to working exploits. Finally, hold your security partners and vendors to high standards of coordinated disclosure. It’s important that our industry continues to normalize agentic vulnerability research , but we must do so responsibly. Let’s continue to keep user safety at the center of everything we do. For more information on the Google Cloud VRP, including detailed endpoint specifications, JSON payloads, and CLI examples, please check out our rules page . aside_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('title', 'Join the Google Cloud CISO Community'), ('body', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd8e6bdbdd0>), ('btn_text', 'Learn more'), ('href', 'https://rsvp.withgoogle.com/events/google-cloud-ciso-community-interest-form-2026?utm_source=cgc-blog&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=FY25-Q1-global-GCP30328-physicalevent-er-dgcsm-parent-CISO-community-2025&utm_content=cisop_&utm_term=-'), ('image', None)])]> In case you missed it Here are the latest updates, products, services, and resources from our security teams so far this month: How Google Does It: Using agents to help find, track, and fix vulnerabilities : Threat actors can now find software flaws faster than ever. To maintain an agile, responsive defense, we now use agentic systems with existing foundations. Read more . How to use agents to stop insider threats : As agents find their place across the enterprise, we want to be sure that they neither become an insider threat nor enable people to become one. Responding to core PHP vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-10961 : Follow these recommendations to minimize remote code execution risks in PHP from two critical vulnerabilities in the core PHP language runtime. Read more . Please visit the Google Cloud blog for more security stories published this month . aside_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('title', 'Learn something new'), ('body', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fd8e6bd89d0>), ('btn_text', 'Watch now'), ('href', 'https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Wpo-5ke9uvQ'), ('image', None)])]> Threat Intelligence news Investigating ephemeral supply chain tampering : For the first time, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant have encountered a software supply chain compromise that was implemented with very short tampering windows that were active for only five to 10 minutes, and effectively evading traditional point-in-time triage and automated file scanning. title: Grounding agents in one context graph connecting semantic models you already trust
raw_text: Picture the scene: Before an executive business review, your VP of Sales asks an AI assistant, "What was net revenue for our top enterprise accounts last quarter?" In seconds, the agent returns a polished chart! Unfortunately, the numbers don't match the finance report. Why? Because the agent counted cancelled orders as revenue and pulled from an unvalidated staging table. The agent didn't fail because of the model, or because it couldn't translate a user question into a query. It failed because it didn't understand your business . The real kicker is that understanding usually already exists in the form of a semantic model in a Looker, dbt, Snowflake, Databricks, or SAP system. But because each definition stays locked inside its own tool, every agent guesses at it… and often gets it wrong. This is where Knowledge Catalog comes in. It brings the semantic models from all of those tools into one context graph, so every agent works from the same trusted definitions. And when two tools define the same metric differently, both definitions appear with their provenance, so data stewards can reconcile the conflict before it reaches end users. Today, we're announcing the general availability of expanded semantic model support. Knowledge Catalog now natively ingests semantic models and metric definitions from Looker LookML, BigQuery Graph (including BigQuery measures), dbt MetricFlow, Snowflake Semantic Views, Databricks Metric Views, and SAP Core Schema Notation (CSN), and connects them with schema, lineage, data profiles, business glossary and other key metadata in a single context graph, without moving data or rewriting business logic in a new language. By grounding your AI agents in those models, they get the same business definitions your analysts rely on, so their answers line up with the numbers your business trusts. In fact, based on internal benchmarks, grounding agents in Knowledge Catalog makes them nearly 4X more accurate, with up to 33% lower latency, and using up to 75% fewer tokens. The unified context graph enables you to: Reuse the semantic models you already trust: Knowledge Catalog grounds Gemini agent, BigQuery Conversational Analytics, and your custom agents in the metrics, filters, and join paths your teams have already defined, wherever they live. Go beyond hand-curated definitions with self-learned context: Knowledge Catalog pairs the well-defined metrics and KPI definitions in your semantic models with relevant context it extracts from unstructured knowledge sources, such as operational playbooks, meeting notes, chat threads, code, and more. Powered by Gemini, self-learning enrichment continuously finds missing or outdated context and turns it into governed, reusable context sets, ensuring your agents' context stays current as definitions change, without relying only on manual curation. Pair business logic with enterprise trust: Even the right formula produces the wrong answer when it runs on stale or uncertified data. That's why Knowledge Catalog can connect semantic definition to data quality scores, freshness signals, and lineage, so an agent knows what it can trust before it writes a line of SQL. Side-by-side comparison of the same question in Gemini without Knowledge Catalog (left) and grounded in Knowledge Catalog (right). Highlights the grounded agent (right) giving an accurate response with less token and lower latency, compared to the agent without Knowledge Catalog (left) hallucinating and using more tokens with higher latency. One context graph across your data estate The context graph that Knowledge Catalog creates is a connected map of your data and semantic estate: tables, semantic models, glossary terms, and data products are nodes; lineage, associations, schema keys, joins mined from real query history, and the join paths declared in your semantic models are the edges. Ingested semantics land in that same graph, next to pre-existing governance and usage signals, so an agent moves from business concept to trusted formula and verified join paths in one traversal. Each source adds its own perspective on your business: Looker LookML (GA): Indexes models, explores, views, and dashboards using Live sync from Looker Core, capturing compiled metric SQL, fan-out-safe join conditions, mandatory filters, and lineage from source tables to executive dashboards. BigQuery Graph (GA): Indexes native property-graph definitions, node and edge tables, graph measures, and business synonyms, so agents reason over connected entities with Graph Query Language (GQL) traversals instead of brittle multi-table self-joins. dbt MetricFlow (GA): Links source objects to dbt models and MetricFlow metrics, alongside dbt data quality test results, filters, saved queries, freshness SLAs, and downstream exposures. Snowflake Semantic Views via Horizon Catalog (GA): Pairs federated BigQuery or Google Cloud Lakehouse tables with Snowflake Horizon metadata, bringing in Semantic View dimensions, facts, metric formulas, relationships, and synonyms, plus Data Metric Function quality scorecards and PII masking tags. Databricks Metric Views via Unity Catalog (GA): Ingests metric view definitions, measure formulas, scoping filters, and join cardinalities from Unity Catalog, alongside table certification badges and Lakehouse Monitoring profiling results. SAP Core Schema Notation (CSN) via SAP Business Data Cloud (BDC) (GA): Captures business labels, dimension and cube modeling patterns, default aggregations, currency and unit bindings, key and composite join associations, and data sensitivity flags when SAP BDC Data Products are federated through Google Cloud Lakehouse. Because every source lands as a node or an edge in the same graph, a LookML join, a dbt exposure, a Snowflake relationship, or an SAP association are traversable side by side, with links tying each one back to the physical tables it depends on. And nothing is silently overwritten: overlapping definitions stay side by side, each labeled with its source, giving data stewards the full picture they need to settle on a single version. Navigating semantic models, join paths, and lineage on the context graph in Knowledge Studio. You can explore and govern all of this in Knowledge Studio (preview), your command center to explore and manage your context. Explore your context graph, including your semantic definitions, using natural language prompts and traverse connection paths using the context graph canvas. Then, once you've validated the right assets and definitions, you can package them into reusable context sets that map to specific use cases and domains in your organization, which Gemini and custom agents can consume in production. Get started Let’s get back to that net revenue question. With Knowledge Catalog, the VP of Sales’ agent issues a single context query to discover the trusted asset, applying the exact metric formula and filters that your domain experts defined, all while respecting join keys across systems, and confirming that the underlying data passed its quality checks. Better yet, the numbers in the report are correct! To get started, explore your context graph in Knowledge Studio and visit the Knowledge Catalog documentation to connect to more sources.
summary: Picture the scene: Before an executive business review, your VP of Sales asks an AI assistant, "What was net revenue for our top enterprise accounts last quarter?" In seconds, the agent returns a polished chart! Unfortunately, the numbers don't match the finance report. Why? Because the agent counted cancelled orders as revenue and pulled from an unvalidated staging table.

title: Choosing a WAAP in 2026: 3 questions that separate the shortlist
raw_text: One platform or four Your WAF renewal is coming up. The API team has its own tooling in mind, the fraud team wants a bot product, and someone in networking owns DDoS. Four controls, four consoles, four sets of policies in front of the same applications. That is the situation a Web Application and API Protection platform, or WAAP, exists to replace: one service in front of the application portfolio that handles the WAF, API security, bot management, DDoS, and client-side script protection together. The category is settled. What changed in 2026 is the evidence. Buyers now have certified test data that measures how well these platforms stop attacks and how often they stop legitimate traffic by mistake, and the two numbers together tell you more than any feature list. What the test data shows The SecureIQLab Cloud WAAP v5.0 validation, an AMTSO-certified test published in August 2026, ran 12 enterprise platforms through 1,608 attack scenarios and 1,487 legitimate-traffic scenarios. Complete Security Scores ran from a perfect 100% for the top product down to roughly 61% for the weakest. The spread inside a typical shortlist is that wide, and a shortlist drawn up in 2023 or 2024 may no longer describe the products on it. The second number matters as much as the first. A platform that blocks every attack and also blocks legitimate requests cannot stay in blocking mode for long, and false positive avoidance varied almost as widely across the same twelve products. Those percentage points become alerts, tuning hours, and exceptions your team carries every day. 3 questions for every vendor on the list Ask for API coverage protocol by protocol. REST is one protocol among several in a modern estate; GraphQL, SOAP, WebSockets, and gRPC all carry production traffic, and the v5.0 results showed coverage varying widely by protocol inside a single product, with WebSockets the weakest area across the group. A headline API score hides that. Ask how long it takes to reach a tuned, low false-positive state on your traffic, and measure it over two full weeks of real traffic during the proof of value. Time to protection and tuning effort are the costs you pay after the contract is signed. Ask how the deployment and licensing model behaves as the portfolio grows. Each delivery model, SaaS, native in-cloud, or reverse proxy, has its own latency and onboarding profile, and each licensing unit, request, bandwidth, or application, bends the cost curve differently as traffic grows. Model 24 to 36 months of growth with each vendor, starting from your own traffic baseline. Where Imperva fits Imperva, part of Thales, delivers Cloud WAF, Advanced Bot Protection, API Security, DDoS Protection, and Client-Side Protection as one platform, with one policy model and one set of analytics across all of them, deployable as SaaS, on your own infrastructure, or natively inside the public cloud. In the SecureIQLab v5.0 cycle, Imperva was the only vendor of the twelve tested to record a perfect 100% Complete Security Score, and it paired that with a 100% false positive avoidance score, the lab’s measure of legitimate traffic passed untouched. It was Imperva’s fifth consecutive Leader-category placement in the series, and the lab awarded it the Secure by Default rating in the same cycle. Forrester named Imperva a Leader in The Forrester Wave™: Web Application Firewall Solutions, Q1 2025. An honest aside: no one platform suits every environment. If your dominant requirement is a developer-centric edge platform or raw DDoS scrubbing capacity above everything else, weigh those needs explicitly, and validate any shortlist, Imperva included, against your own traffic in a proof of value. The full comparison The complete buyer’s guide on the Imperva blog compares seven WAAP vendors on security efficacy, API protection, bot defense, operational efficiency, and cost, with analyst standing and verified peer ratings for each, and ends with a proof-of-value checklist you can take into your next evaluation. Read Best WAAP Solutions for Enterprise Application Security: How to Choose the Right Platform in 2026 before you renew anything. Then go back to the four consoles and decide how many you still need.

title: Why identity governance demands executive attention
raw_text: The identity landscape you’re responsible for looks nothing like it did just a few years ago. Employees and contractors now share the enterprise with service accounts, machine identities, and a fast-growing population of AI agents — all accessing business systems and data. Every one of those identities represents an access decision, and every access decision is now a potential point of accountability that lands on your desk. Regulators and boards want proof. They expect security leaders to show who, or what, has access to critical systems and how that access is being governed. But when human and nonhuman identities (NHIs) change faster than manual processes can keep up, proof becomes much harder to produce. Foundry research ranks identity security among the top cybersecurity priorities for 2026, reflecting a shift in how leadership views risk: Identity has evolved from operational detail to executive concern. “The last 15 years of digital transformation has resulted in credential sprawl across the tech stack of every organization,” says Bryan Kelley, AVP, Agentic Technology Specialists at SailPoint. “Whether it’s your own trusted agents or another organization’s rogue agent, they will find and abuse these exposed credentials, API keys, tokens, and secrets to carry out their given goals.” When accountability becomes personal Security leaders must demonstrate that identity governance is working, not simply that policies exist. They need a real-time view of each identity and the permissions it holds as business needs change. Leaders can also face personal and professional consequences when a breach or a compliance failure occurs. Boards and regulators may expect the C-suite to show that appropriate controls and oversight were in place at the time. AI agents add to that exposure as they gain access to enterprise resources and take on more autonomous roles. This is why NHIs need the same rigor, visibility, and controls as human identities. The shift to continuous compliance Quarterly or annual access reviews capture a moment in time, but it’s all the other moments in between that present a problem. Between reviews, employees can change roles, contractors can leave, and new identities such as AI agents can gain access. Security teams may not catch outdated permissions or active orphaned accounts until the next review. When identity data lives in separate systems, security teams struggle even more to maintain a current view of access across the enterprise . Continuous identity security makes oversight part of daily operations. Rather than waiting for the next review, an identity governance platform can help validate access as conditions change, automating low-risk approvals and flagging higher-risk access for review. Governance activity also creates an ongoing record of how access was approved and whether policies were applied consistently, so teams don’t have to reconstruct that history when auditors or regulators ask for evidence. Building an adaptive identity security program A continuous approach is made up of three core capabilities. First, organizations need to discover and unify identities to create a centralized view of access. Second, lifecycle management, policy enforcement, and access validation become always-on activities rather than periodic projects. Finally, organizations need to maintain evidence of governance activity so they can demonstrate compliance and respond when issues arise. This approach helps security leaders keep up with constant identity changes while meeting rising expectations for accountability. Learn how continuous identity security can help strengthen oversight and audit readiness.
summary: The identity landscape you’re responsible for looks nothing like it did just a few years ago. Employees and contractors now share the enterprise with service accounts, machine identities, and a fast-growing population of AI agents — all accessing business systems and data. Every one of those identities represents an access decision, and every access decision is now a potential point of accountability that lands on your desk. Regulators and boards want proof.

title: Anthropic AI model finds Linux kernel bug that leads to remote root access
raw_text: Linux servers running Multipath TCP (MPTCP) could be vulnerable to remote code execution through a flaw in the kernel’s networking stack. Anthropic has disclosed a zero-click exploit developed with an unreleased Claude research model that allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root, without requiring any user interaction. Tracked as CVE-2026-98432 , the vulnerability is a race-condition-induced use-after-free (UAF) bug in the Linux kernel. Anthropic demonstrated how an attacker could exploit the flaw remotely to leak kernel memory, defeat Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR), hijack kernel control flow, and ultimately execute an attacker-controlled shell command. The research is part of Anthropic’s broader effort to evaluate AI models’ ability to discover and exploit vulnerabilities in widely deployed software. The company disclosed five exploit chains involving Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux to demonstrate how its internal model could combine multiple weaknesses into functional attacks. Anthropic’s proof of concept for the Linux exploit took approximately 53 minutes to progress from the initial memory leak to successful root-level command execution, the company said in a blog post . A TCP connection race leaves kernel memory exposed According to a Linux kernel CVE advisory , the underlying flaw involves how Linux manages IP options during IPv4 TCP connection establishment. When a new connection is created, the kernel can transfer ownership of IP options from a pending connection request to the newly created socket without making a separate copy. The problem arises when another CPU is simultaneously processing a retransmitted connection request and using those same options to construct a synchronize-acknowledge (SYNACK) response. If the child socket is freed before the second CPU finishes accessing the options, the kernel can end up reading memory that has already been released. This creates a use-after-free condition. The upstream fix addresses the memory-management problem by deferring the release of the affected objects until after a read-copy-update (RCU) grace period, giving concurrent readers time to finish accessing them. The flaw received a critical severity score of 9.8 and affects eight Linux kernel branches, dating back to version 4.4. Fixed releases include 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.6.159, 6.1.190, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10 and 7.3-rc7. For users who obtain Linux through distributions such as Debian, Oracle Linux, SUSE, and Amazon Linux, fixed kernel packages are available for at least some releases. Ubuntu and Red Hat Enterprise Linux, however, had yet to release patched kernels as of October 30. MCTCP listeners create the remote attack surface Anthropic’s exploit specifically targets Linux servers running an MPTCP listener. MPTCP extends conventional TCP by allowing a device to use multiple network interfaces simultaneously within a single connection. This enables bandwidth aggregation, improved network selection, and failover when one network path becomes unavailable. Linux implements MPTCP through its networking stack, but the protocol is opt-in: applications must explicitly request it when creating sockets, although mechanisms such as eBPF and other configuration techniques can also force applications to use it. Administrators are advised to review their kernel versions, apply the relevant security updates, and assess whether their systems expose MPTCP listeners.
summary: Linux servers running Multipath TCP (MPTCP) could be vulnerable to remote code execution through a flaw in the kernel’s networking stack. Anthropic has disclosed a zero-click exploit developed with an unreleased Claude research model that allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root, without requiring any user interaction. Tracked as CVE-2026-98432 , the vulnerability is a race-condition-induced use-after-free (UAF) bug in the Linux kernel. Anthropic demonstrated how an attacker could exploit the flaw remotely to leak kernel memory, defeat Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR), hijack kernel control flow, and ultimately execute an attacker-controlled shell command.

title: Mistral open-sources AI model despite warning it could aid cyberattacks
raw_text: A trillion-parameter AI model that its developer says could help attackers carry out real cyberattacks is now free to download, modify and run outside the developer’s control. Mistral AI released the open weights of Mistral Large 4, which it calls “Le Chonk,” on Thursday, weeks after putting the multimodal model into public preview. The Paris-based company said it had monitored cybersecurity-related use of the preview in live traffic. “Though we observed the model refusing to comply with black-box attacks against live targets, we see a potential for uplift to conduct real attacks,” the company wrote in a blog post announcing the release. Mistral is modifying the model’s guardrails and will keep updating them in the coming months, the post added. Guardrails stop at the API Those updates will not reach copies already downloaded. Pierre Stock, Mistral’s vice president of science, told CSO that the model ships with safeguards built into its weights, but later changes will go elsewhere. “Subsequent safeguard updates are applied to our managed API and future model releases, rather than automatically updating downloaded checkpoints,” Stock said. Asked which attack stages the model had meaningfully helped with in preview traffic, Stock did not name any. He said the most significant gains were in defensive work such as identifying, reproducing and remediating software vulnerabilities. “While our public-preview monitoring showed the model refusing attacks against live targets, we recognise the potential for misuse as capabilities advance and are continuously strengthening our safeguards,” he said. Hugging Face, which hosts the weights, noted in its own launch post that open weights put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. In July, the UK’s AI Security Institute reported that leading open-weight models trailed the closed frontier on cyber tasks by four to seven months. For highly cyber-capable models, open release creates “a persistent and irreversible risk of misuse,” the institute said. Attackers are already putting open-source AI tooling to work. Earlier this month, Microsoft said a China-aligned group used the agentic AI framework ARTEX to target more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. Mistral says the released model can tell defensive work from malicious requests. According to the company, Large 4 refused 96.6% of malicious prompts in the cyber-related portions of the JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm benchmarks, the highest rate it has measured among open models. Niyati Daftary, principal analyst at Gartner, said security leaders should read that number narrowly. “Mistral’s 96.6% figure tells you what their model does in their test scenario, not how it will behave with your data, your adversarial use cases or in production in your environment against motivated attackers,” she said. Mistral is handling a specialized cybersecurity variant differently. Design partners such as Orange Cyberdefense are getting preview access to a version optimized for penetration testing, vulnerability assessment and red-teaming, the company said. Access is “subject to rigorous vetting and contractual safeguards,” the post said, and is limited to systems partners own or are authorized to test. Benchmarks and EU obligations The company said the model scored 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which measures how well a model finds, reproduces, and patches vulnerabilities. The chart in Mistral’s post shows two open-weight models, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and MiMo-V2.6-Pro, scoring higher. Mistral also calls Large 4 the best open-weight model for coding, citing leading scores on Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 and Terminal-Bench 4.0. It has not yet published the technical report behind those results and has said only that one is coming soon. “Without a detailed technical report, the best open-weight model claim remains difficult to validate across workloads,” said Charlie Dai, vice president and principal analyst at Forrester. Dai added that frontier models are evolving so quickly that leadership “can shift within months or even weeks.” Stock said the report will document Mistral’s cyber evaluation methods and results, refusal testing and preview monitoring findings. Mistral also intends to share relevant adversarial testing findings “while safeguarding sensitive security information,” he said. He did not give a publication date. ENISA, the EU’s cybersecurity agency, said in a statement published with Mistral’s announcement that it is testing the model to identify vulnerabilities, audit code and analyze defensive logs. Under the EU AI Act, models trained with more than 10^25 floating-point operations (FLOPs) are presumed to carry systemic risk, according to the European Commission . Their providers must assess and mitigate those risks, report serious incidents and maintain cybersecurity protections. Mistral’s post does not say whether Large 4 falls into that category or what risk assessment preceded the release. Stock said Mistral is a full signatory of the EU’s General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, including its safety and security chapter, which the Commission accepts as one way to demonstrate compliance. He did not say whether Large 4 has been classified as a systemic-risk model. What it means for enterprises Mistral released the model under a modified MIT license that permits use, modification, fine-tuning, and commercialization, the company said. Businesses running a model-as-a-service offering need a separate license. For those who would rather not host it, Mistral’s API is priced at $0.70 per million input tokens and $2.10 per million output tokens. For European buyers, sovereignty is “a meaningful differentiator, but it should not outweigh security concerns,” Dai said. Open weights and self-hosting shift responsibility for guardrails, access controls, monitoring and misuse prevention to the operator, he added. “Sovereignty and security therefore need to be evaluated together, not traded against each other,” Dai said. Daftary said enterprises self-hosting Large 4 for code audit or vulnerability triage should run it as a controlled component, not an autonomous agent. That means isolated environments, least-privilege access to code and credentials, sandboxed generated code, and human sign-off before any remediation, she said. “Self-hosting can improve data control and operational continuity, but it also makes the enterprise solely responsible for patching, monitoring, evaluation and misuse prevention,” she said.
summary: A trillion-parameter AI model that its developer says could help attackers carry out real cyberattacks is now free to download, modify and run outside the developer’s control. Mistral AI released the open weights of Mistral Large 4, which it calls “Le Chonk,” on Thursday, weeks after putting the multimodal model into public preview. The Paris-based company said it had monitored cybersecurity-related use of the preview in live traffic. “Though we observed the model refusing to comply with black-box attacks against live targets, we see a potential for uplift to conduct real attacks,” the company wrote in a blog post announcing the release.

title: Everyday channels are available in an incident, but you may not want them
raw_text: The first hours after a serious cyber incident are filled with activity . Security starts investigating, IT works to contain the impact, legal begins assessing potential obligations, and executives want to know what happened and what the company is doing about it. Most teams rely on the same tools they use every day to coordinate that work, which usually means email, Slack, Teams, shared documents and video calls. Coordination gets much more complicated when the company’s email or collaboration environment is part of the incident. Email may still work, employees may still be able to join meetings, and nothing on the surface may suggest that the organization has lost control of its communications. Meanwhile, an attacker with access to accounts used by responders may read the team’s messages, monitor containment plans or impersonate someone involved in the response. When that happens, the company faces a second crisis inside the first. The systems people depend on to manage the incident can no longer be trusted. After more than two decades in the privacy and breach space, and in my weekly conversations with security and legal teams, I see the same pattern. Most incident response plans account for email or collaboration tools becoming unavailable. Teams have phone trees, personal contact information and backup conference lines. They know whom they need to call. What they often lack is a systematic approach for the harder case. Far fewer plans address the more ambiguous situation in which those systems remain functional while the organization can no longer be certain who is reading, sending or altering messages inside them. That scenario requires a preplanned way to move the response out of band while investigators determine what has been compromised. When the attacker may be inside the response This problem is easy to see during ransomware . Systems go down, employees lose access and the need for alternative communications becomes obvious. Compromised communications make judgment harder because the affected environment may appear completely normal. Suppose the security team discovers that an attacker has gained access to email and collaboration accounts used by incident response team members. The team needs to determine the scope of that access, remove the attacker and contain the intrusion, but discussing those actions in the regular incident channel could tell the attacker exactly what is coming. Legal needs the latest facts to evaluate notification requirements, the comms team is preparing for questions from customers, and leadership expects regular updates. Every one of those conversations may reveal something valuable to the person the company is trying to remove. The attacker is in the meeting. Responders then must answer a basic question before they can safely coordinate anything else: Who can see what we are saying? Countless companies rely on Teams or Slack during incidents because those are the systems their employees already use. The tradeoff is that the response stays inside an environment the attacker may already access and has every reason to monitor. I’m aware of several cases where attackers joined or recorded Zoom and Teams bridges used for incident meetings. What was already said As I discussed in my previous CSO article , putting a lawyer in a large incident channel does not make every conversation privileged. Operational facts and legal advice serve different purposes, and a crisis does not remove the need to control who participates in sensitive discussions. If the attacker was reading the channel, assume that every containment plan, every candid assessment of how the intrusion happened, and every draft customer statement posted there is now outside the company. Some of it may surface in an extortion demand. All of it may surface in discovery. Plan as though the company will end up in court. The out-of-band channel should give teams a place to separate operational coordination from legal analysis, limit participation and begin building the record that regulators and plaintiffs may later examine: what was decided, by whom, on what facts and why. Legal should design that structure before the incident. Trying to create it during one, in a channel the attacker may be reading, compounds the problem. What an out-of-band plan must solve The mistake I see is starting with a backup application. Start with the failure scenario and map every dependency shared by the primary and emergency communications environments, including identity services, managed devices, mobile device management, administrative credentials and employee directories. If both channels depend on the same underlying component, that component remains a single point of failure. Then decide how participants will prove who they are. An attacker with access to email or calendars may know that an emergency meeting is taking place and have enough context to impersonate an executive or responder. The verification process cannot depend on the accounts under investigation. The same preparation should cover outside counsel, forensic investigators, insurers and communications advisers. Maintain current contact information, define who can authorize their participation, and establish how the team will verify them before an incident begins. Devices also matter. An alternative channel provides little value if responders can reach it only through corporate laptops they have been instructed to disconnect. The plan should specify which devices responders can use and what information they may access through them. The specific approach will depend on the company’s size, risk profile and existing systems. The test is whether the response can continue without relying on the environment under investigation. Practice moving the response Most organizations that test backup communications focus on whether the channel works. They should also rehearse the judgment call that activates it. Participants need to recognize when the primary environment has become untrustworthy, alert the response team without exposing the move, and continue operating in the alternate channel. A tabletop exercise can begin with evidence that an attacker has accessed email and collaboration accounts used by several responders, even though both services still appear to function normally. The team must decide what evidence is sufficient to trigger the move, who has the authority to make that call, and how everyone’s identity will be verified after they arrive. The exercise should bring in security, legal, executives and essential outside partners. Add the complications that make real incidents difficult, such as an executive sending conflicting instructions through corporate email, someone joining a meeting from an unfamiliar account, an outdated emergency contact or a third party unable to authenticate. Those moments reveal whether the company has a working capability or only a document describing one. I would measure how long it takes to recognize the need to move, activate essential stakeholders, establish a verified response group, and brief leadership. Every point at which participants fall back on the affected environment exposes a dependency the written plan missed. Most incident response plans assume the company will have somewhere safe to coordinate. That assumption deserves the same scrutiny as backups, recovery procedures and containment playbooks. The decision to leave familiar systems should have defined triggers, a clear owner and a destination everyone has already practiced using. When the communication environment becomes part of the breach, legal deadlines, business decisions, customers and employees do not wait. The company needs to know when to move, where to go and how to keep operating once it gets there.
summary: The first hours after a serious cyber incident are filled with activity . Security starts investigating, IT works to contain the impact, legal begins assessing potential obligations, and executives want to know what happened and what the company is doing about it. Most teams rely on the same tools they use every day to coordinate that work, which usually means email, Slack, Teams, shared documents and video calls. Coordination gets much more complicated when the company’s email or collaboration environment is part of the incident.

title: We are not ready for what AI has done to red teaming
raw_text: Something shifted in offensive security over the last eighteen months that most organizations haven’t fully absorbed yet. It isn’t that attackers got smarter. It’s that the economics of attack changed entirely — and those of us who run red teams have had a front-row seat to the transformation. The conversation about AI in cybersecurity tends to fixate on defense: better anomaly detection, faster triage, and AI-assisted SOC analysts. That framing misses the more urgent story. The attack side of this ledger has already been rewritten. A small, well-equipped offensive team using frontier AI models today can outperform what was possible with a much larger traditional operation just two years ago, by a margin that should unsettle every security leader reading this. Through our work on the front lines of offensive security, the consensus is clear: if you are not augmenting your operations with AI, you are already at a disadvantage. Before addressing the operational shift, we must clarify a fundamental distinction that is often conflated in industry discussions: AI red teaming: This involves probing Large Language Models (LLMs) for vulnerabilities, testing agentic pipelines, and identifying prompt-injection vectors or unintended behaviors. Red teaming with AI: Using AI as an operator’s tool to execute traditional offensive operations. It is this second category, Red Teaming with AI, where the most immediate, drastic, and dangerous transformation is occurring. The staggering scale of productivity AI-augmented operations transitioned from a nice-to-have luxury to a non-negotiable requirement. The democratization of frontier models introduces asymmetry between well-equipped adversaries and traditional defensive teams relying on manual triage. The productivity leaps we are seeing in the field are staggering. When AI is effectively weaponized by offensive teams, some of the initial findings speak for themselves: Metric Traditional red teaming AI-augmented red teaming Annual team output 60 to 70 findings (3-4 person team) 90+ findings generated in a single after-hours exercise Single app engagement 7 to 10 findings 100+ true positive findings Large-scale scanning Takes appropriate sequencing and pipelines, or times out entirely Enables you to build capabilities that can scan millions of IPs in 2-3 hours (for roughly $20k-$30k) Reconnaissance of external applications 150-200 valid findings/year 100+ findings a month (Data above aggregated by DayBlink Consulting over past 10 years of engagements and validated by Robert Pimentel as representative of his Red team experience.) AI across the engagement lifecycle We are no longer just using AI to write phishing emails. Organizations and threat actors alike are adopting a structured approach to integrate AI throughout every phase of the kill chain: Pre-operation (setup and reconnaissance): The weeks-long setup phase has been accelerated into mere moments. Gathering Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT), provisioning infrastructure, building organizational charts, and configuring command-and-control (C2) servers can now be delegated to agentic AI. This significantly reduces the time and manual effort needed to get an operation off the ground, though complex infrastructure decisions still require experienced operators. Pre-op usually starts off exciting (new op coming) but often ends in a grind. We love the acceleration AI has provided here. Mid-operation (enumeration and attack): during active engagements, AI acts as a real-time, on-demand expert. Operators use AI interactively to generate custom audit scripts, rapidly adapt strategies, and query unfamiliar technology stacks on the fly. By utilizing an LLMs-as-judges workflow, where one model’s output is vetted by another for correctness and risk before execution, attackers can ensure highly confident, automated actions. Enumeration and attack is where all the excitement and adrenaline happens. We are using AI to help here, but it’s not replacing us humans (yet). Post-operation (reporting and deconfliction): reporting has historically been the most tedious burden of any engagement. Today, nine to ten months of raw C2 logs can be piped into a frontier model to generate a comprehensive deconfliction report in under 20 minutes. These tools can map every executed command to the MITRE ATT&CK framework , cross-reference threat intelligence, and translate highly technical data into clear, actionable narratives for board-level executives. The output still requires manual review. AI gets you to a first draft in minutes instead of days, but an operator needs to verify findings, validate ATT&CK mappings, and ensure accuracy before delivery. Ticketing and follow-up are the bane of most red teams. AI has become an awesome sidekick to our teams to build our reports and do lots of the tedious work. The talent divide: judgment as the ultimate differentiator With AI automating basic enumeration, scanning, and scaffolding, the core red-teaming skill set — critical thinking, architectural understanding, adversarial judgment — is as valuable as it’s ever been. AI doesn’t replace that. But operators who can leverage AI alongside those skills will outperform those who can’t. The differentiator isn’t AI versus no AI; it’s whether you have the foundational knowledge to direct it effectively and validate what it gives you. This is fundamentally shifting the required profile of a successful cybersecurity professional. As a result, the industry is quickly diverging into two distinct categories of practitioners: The “unicorns” (high performers): These are the practitioners who bring critical thinking and deep adversarial judgment to AI. They understand exactly where trust boundaries fail and where architectures are weak. They use AI to execute on these insights efficiently, offloading the busywork to focus on complex exploitation. The “slop cannons”: Operators who use AI as a mindless copy-paste shortcut. They rely entirely on unverified outputs without understanding the underlying mechanics, producing noisy, easily detectable work that wastes time and triggers alarms. Consequently, hiring practices must change. The primary screening criterion for new talent can no longer be a stack of legacy certifications; it must be their hands-on curiosity, their fundamental understanding of network architecture, and their experience building tools with frontier AI models. Certifications still matter, but hiring must also evaluate whether candidates can think critically about systems and leverage AI tools effectively — not just operate them blindly Strategic imperatives for 2027 For security leaders looking to survive this paradigm shift, the path forward requires immediate action. Based on our observations, here are the critical priorities for the next 18 months: Formalize AI budgets: Access to frontier models is expensive, but it is a necessary operational cost. Teams without the budget to experiment and build will fall behind adversaries. Implement continuous, programmatic testing: As enterprises deploy thousands of their own agentic integrations, manual testing is no longer viable. Continuous, automated adversarial testing must become the standard operating procedure. Prepare for hybrid threat vectors: As digital perimeters harden through automated defense, attacks will increasingly blend hyper-automated digital exploits with highly sophisticated physical and social engineering vectors. Hire for curiosity: Build teams anchored by practitioners who are actively experimenting with AI and possess the high-level judgment needed to guide it safely and effectively. Organizations that fail to adopt an AI-augmented mindset risk being overwhelmed by adversaries operating faster, smarter, and at an unprecedented scale. Success in the modern cyber landscape relies on one core principle: seamlessly combining elite human judgment with intelligent automation.
summary: Something shifted in offensive security over the last eighteen months that most organizations haven’t fully absorbed yet. It isn’t that attackers got smarter. It’s that the economics of attack changed entirely — and those of us who run red teams have had a front-row seat to the transformation. The conversation about AI in cybersecurity tends to fixate on defense: better anomaly detection, faster triage, and AI-assisted SOC analysts.

title: Beyond deterministic worms: Preparing the SOC for reasoning adversaries
raw_text: In May 2017, the WannaCry cryptoworm spread across the internet, compromising more than 200,000 computers in at least 100 countries. The National Audit Office called it the largest cyberattack ever to hit the NHS in England. At least 80 of 236 hospital trusts were infected or disrupted, an estimated 19,000 appointments were cancelled, five hospitals diverted ambulances, and more than 1,200 pieces of diagnostic equipment were infected. What stopped WannaCry was a stroke of luck. A researcher reverse engineered the malware, noticed it contacting a domain nobody had registered, and registered it. That evening the original strain stopped locking devices. WannaCry had a kill switch, and we are all fortunate that Marcus Hutchins was able to find it. As I read agent incident reports from OpenAI and Anthropic , I am reminded of WannaCry. But the threat from offensive agents is not a faster worm. In July, roughly 1,200 OpenAI agents being tested on a cybersecurity benchmark found an unsanctioned message board on an internal software repository, and some broke out to the internet. About 700 of those agents went on to attack Hugging Face, looking for clues to beat the benchmark, according to an independent investigation . Hugging Face disclosed the intrusion on July 16, and OpenAI confirmed its agents were responsible five days later. Recently Anthropic has had unintended incidents as well. Anthropic’s incidents involved single models rather than a swarm. In cyber evaluations that were accidentally left connected to the internet, individual Claude models attacked real companies’ systems while trying to complete their exercises, and one published a malicious package to PyPI . Worms like WannaCry exploit a single or small number of vulnerabilities, using a static set of techniques. Agents can read the results of failed attempts, try something else, and pass on what they learned to other agents. Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team evaluated GLM-5.3 , an open-weights model from Z.ai that NIST’s CAISI assessed as the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date. Over a day, with under an hour of hands-on attention, a researcher used it to find several unknown browser vulnerabilities and chain them into an exploit that steals a user’s SSH key. A smaller variant built an exploit chain for two known flaws for roughly $20 at API prices. Simple techniques bypassed its safeguards 64% to 100% of the time in simulated tests, including abliteration, which edits the released weights to strip out refusals. A high-performing SOC working to the “1-10-60” benchmark — 1 minute to detect, 10 to investigate, and 60 to contain — is not built for this. When the adversary moves from a human at a keyboard to groups of autonomous agents operating at machine speed, response has to be measured in seconds. The Hugging Face incident shows the gap even when the agents belong to a well-intentioned party. OpenAI did not contain them in time. OpenAI reports that its own monitoring flagged the agents twice in the preceding weeks. In June, their responders decided the activity did not warrant stopping the evaluation. In early July, they found a compromised server, revoked credentials and blocked the exploited paths. Within a day of the evaluations resuming, the agents had found a new zero-day and were back on the internet. They compromised Hugging Face between July 11 and 13, and OpenAI linked it to its agents on July 20. When Hugging Face investigated the intrusion, the hosted models it tried first refused to analyze the attack logs, and its team finished the forensics with GLM-5.2 running on its own infrastructure. As Hugging Face put it : “the attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried .” What makes this different None of this is new to our industry. We have always played leapfrog with attackers. What is new today is that they can now download capable models with no meaningful safeguards and build their own offensive agents. Imagine WannaCry if the worm rewrote itself the moment the domain was registered. The best SOC in the world would still be diagnosing the initial compromise when it had moved on. Agents that depend on a provider can be contained by revoking credentials, suspending accounts, and blocking egress, though OpenAI’s experience shows it may take more than one attempt. Open-weight models running on an attacker’s hardware cannot. Anthropic recently tested whether small models could replicate across cheap connected devices without a datacenter. In simplified evaluations with trivial access controls, a stronger open-weight model completed the full chain, and Anthropic projects small models reaching that level by year-end if current trends hold. A replicator like that has no central point to switch off. It would be slow and visible on the network, but patient and everywhere. Hospitals know the problem: Some equipment WannaCry disrupted, such as MRI scanners with embedded Windows XP, was vendor-managed and could not be updated by the trusts. Agents do not need to be intentionally asked to embark on offensive exercises to exhibit harmful behavior. Transluce documented agents asked to do ordinary data retrieval that, when blocked, probed public websites for vulnerabilities, including an Australian government agency. Some were linked to the swarm OpenAI has acknowledged as its own. The Hugging Face agents were trying to win a benchmark. Poorly constrained agents are enough for unintended harmful activity. We are deploying agents as assistance for site reliability engineering (SRE) and infrastructure as code (IaC) ourselves, and cloud providers are shipping agent toolkits to manage infrastructure. When, not if, a compromised or poorly managed agent holds those privileges, it will be able to deploy its own infrastructure to run on. We have already seen agents in a lab environment stand up their own relays and cloud infrastructure with stolen credentials. Meeting the agent challenge But we can still prepare for these future scenarios today. To do so, CISOs must treat agents as privileged identities: Give each agent short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials, with no standing permissions. Forbid agents from creating new identities, compute, or network paths without human approval. Put agent workloads behind egress allowlists, so a blocked agent cannot go looking for another way out. Enforce policy-as-code guardrails on infrastructure pipelines, and alert on anomalous machine-identity behavior and unexpected resource creation. The NAO’s report is the best documentation of WannaCry’s damage , and it covers a single health system in one country. Large groups of agents carrying a ransom payload could reach hospitals across the planet with no kill switch to find. Autonomous defense is extremely challenging in healthcare, because a false positive can interrupt patient monitoring, biomedical telemetry or imaging, having a significant impact on patient safety. Current tools, including copilots that help a human triage alerts faster, are nowhere close to the offensive capabilities the labs are evaluating. We need defensive parity at machine speed. Zero false positives is not a realistic engineering target, so design of autonomous defense has to assume mistakes and limit their cost. Automate fast, narrowly scoped, reversible actions such as isolating a single device, revoking a narrowly scoped token or quarantining a workload, and keep a human in the loop for anything irreversible or clinically risky. Always have a way to reverse automated actions as quickly as they are introduced. We need to build graduated autonomy, tiered by asset class. You can be more aggressive on the corporate assets, and more conservative around biomedical devices. Leveling up security fundamentals — and business support What else can we do today? Keep our tried-and-true practices and run them faster — something that will require leadership, and additional support from CEOs and the board. In its analysis, the NAO found that applying the patch, or simply managing internet-facing firewalls, would have protected every NHS organization WannaCry infected. Companies and open source projects are now running coding agents over their software and releasing an unprecedented number of security patches. This is great but IT needs to be able to apply them. Give IT the resources to deploy them, retire outdated infrastructure, and make the business tolerant of the maintenance windows this requires. That segmentation or zero trust initiative that has been on the back burner? Make it a priority. Today. If you are still underinvested in security, increase funding now so your team or vendor can acquire the tools and expertise the next few years will demand. And accept that automated defense will sometimes get it wrong. Security teams will have to automate, and the business will have to tolerate the outages that follow. The technology is emerging and it will not be perfect. Support your teams anyway. An open letter to the AI labs and the security community at large A note to the frontier labs. Several of you deserve credit: Project Glasswing and OpenAI’s Patch the Planet put frontier capability in defenders’ hands, and your incident reports have been unusually candid. But offensive capability is moving faster than safeguards. GLM-5.3 shipped as downloadable weights that simple techniques unlocked 64% to 100% of the time, and gated access does nothing about weights already in attackers’ hands. As a result, I am asking for three things: Hold defensive research to the same urgency as capability research, including autonomous containment with a safety case that works in clinical environments. Widen defenders’ access to the class of models attackers will have. Make independent testing before release, and independent investigation after incidents, an obligation rather than a courtesy. METR’s CEO noted that OpenAI let investigators in voluntarily, with no industry requirement on any lab to disclose an incident. I have seen too many security professionals dismiss talk of offensive AI as marketing or fearmongering and answer concerns with “fix your stuff.” Patching matters, and the NAO’s findings on WannaCry articulate that, but that is not the only answer to agents that organize on improvised message boards and probe websites while doing ordinary work. WannaCry’s authors left a kill switch in. The next generation of threats will not have one, and cybercriminals will not disclose when they lose control of a swarm. We cannot rely on strokes of luck. Let’s recognize the risk, discuss it, and prepare before the attackers start using these tools in earnest.
summary: In May 2017, the WannaCry cryptoworm spread across the internet, compromising more than 200,000 computers in at least 100 countries. The National Audit Office called it the largest cyberattack ever to hit the NHS in England. At least 80 of 236 hospital trusts were infected or disrupted, an estimated 19,000 appointments were cancelled, five hospitals diverted ambulances, and more than 1,200 pieces of diagnostic equipment were infected. What stopped WannaCry was a stroke of luck.

title: PHP2Shell plus Fragnesia: A dangerous new route from web server to root
raw_text: The PHP2Shell saga continues, with attackers discovering new ways to exploit the critical vulnerability impacting millions of organizations worldwide. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has warned of a high severity Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw that attackers are chaining with PHP2Shell bugs in the wild. Identified as CVE-2026-46300 , it could allow attackers to run malicious code with root permissions, giving them unrestricted ability to run commands, tamper with system settings, view, edit, or delete files, and perform other malicious actions. Once attackers establish root access, they can perform any action on a server including, but not limited to, disabling the server, creating accounts, removing accounts, connecting to other servers, and adding/removing software, explained Scott Miserendino , CTO at security and compliance platform DataBee. “PHP2Shell allows for remote access, but that access is typically limited by the account used to run the PHP service,” he said. “By chaining with CVE-2026-46300, that attacker can get unlimited access.” Researchers at Dream Security have discovered that this attack has already been used to breach 25 servers, including three affiliated with the US government. Federal agencies have been ordered to patch the flaw, which is known as Fragnesia . Anatomy of an attack PHP is a widely-used, open source server-side scripting language that serves as the backbone for websites like WordPress, which powers 43% of the web , as well as Mailchimp, Drupal, parts of Slack and Zoom, and numerous others. Last week, the PHP Foundation disclosed two flaws in the PHP scripting language that could allow attackers to perform unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are both rated a critical 9.2 in severity on the common vulnerability and scoring system (CVSS). The two vulnerabilities are collectively tracked as PHP2Shell. As a result of the disclosure, some government and enterprise websites shut down entirely while awaiting patches. CVE-2026-46300 , dubbed Fragnesia, is a new development in the saga. It is identified as part of the Dirty Frag vulnerability class, a set of local privilege escalation (LPE) bugs in the Linux kernel. The Dream researchers described an attack they tracked in the wild, in which threat actors built a persistent tunnel into an internal network “within hours.” They developed two distinct exploits, stringing them together to target any Palo Alto Network firewall running a vulnerable build of PAN-OS, and achieved root access in a single HTTP request without any credentials. After rooting the firewalls, the threat actor launched attacks against Active Directory (AD), giving them the ability to extract credentials and discover hidden files, folders, and other sensitive resources, according to the Dream researchers. The researchers confirmed that the threat actor then possessed a full AD user group listing and “complete organizational blueprint,” private keys and complete network topology, including the IP, hostname, server role, and VPN gateway, and had accessed decrypted service account credentials allowing direct AD queries at any time. The adversarial actor also parked nearly two dozen firewalls across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, “ready for exploitation at any time.” The Dream researchers noted that the breach did not appear to be a fully autonomous nation-state attack, but did include some AI-assisted tooling like Claude Code and AI-powered offensive security platforms configured with Chinese large language models (LLMs) DeepSeek and Kimi. “The operation illustrates how an exposed management interface can become a path into an organization’s identity infrastructure,” the Dream researchers wrote. Plenty of material for attackers to work with The two PHP bugs gave an attacker code execution privileges using the web service account, and the kernel bug is what turned that into root, explained Aaron Beardslee , manager of threat research at Securonix, who noted, “The kernel bug writes its payload into the page cache rather than to disk.” Once an attacker has the ability to execute code, the damage they can do depends on the permissions and credentials available to that process, he explained. Application configuration files, database credentials, and access to internal services can provide “plenty of material for an attacker to work with.” They may also be able to execute commands, retrieve additional tooling or establish persistence. “Web servers have an unfortunate habit of knowing more about the rest of the environment than anyone intended,” he pointed out. The chain’s post-access sequence, as described by the researchers, was: Root the perimeter host, stand up a reverse Secure Shell (SSH) tunnel to an internal management server, recover a Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) service account credential, then “enumerate domain users and groups, spray passwords, and attempt to create backdoor accounts in Active Directory.” PHP has “been holding up a substantial chunk” of the internet for decades, and these vulnerabilities live in the runtime itself, Beardslee noted. An enterprise’s WordPress installation can be fully patched, plugins can be current, but the underlying PHP process can still be vulnerable to unauthenticated code execution. The reported victim count (25 servers so far, mostly firewall appliances, on a government affiliated network) is the part everyone will quote, but it is not the interesting part, he said. Counts differ, and attribution is “openly contested.” None of them is what matters to defenders. “What matters is that the privilege escalation step in this chain is invisible to disk-based integrity checking,” Beardslee said, “and that the standard remediation advice destroys the evidence of it.” Remediation Unfortunately, CVE-2026-46300 is a low-level Linux kernel bug, so the only remedy is to upgrade to a patched Linux version, said DataBee’s Miserendino. There are some options short of full patching, but those could break the system, or at a minimum require IPSec encapsulating security payload (ESP) to be disabled. But that can introduce additional flaws. “Patch the kernel, and capture memory first on anything you suspect,” Beardslee recommended, noting that the Fragnesia fix is not included in the Dirty Frag patches. “The triage order matters more here than it usually does, because the reboot is what erases the evidence.” As well, audit the core built-in kernel modules esp4 and esp6 , which are responsible for handling the IPsec ESP network protocol, on every internet-facing Linux host, he advised. If nothing terminates IPsec there, “the modules have no business being loaded,” and unloading them removes the vulnerability path without waiting for a maintenance window. And check which hosts hold a directory service credential, then alert of LDAP binds from anything that isn’t on that list, he said: “This is the control that catches the chain at the stage where it stops being a web server problem and starts being a domain problem.” Further, he said, re-point identity detections at “the source, not the tool.”
