Identified as CVE-2026-46300 , it could allow attackers to run malicious code with root permissions, giving them unrestricted ability to run commands, tamper with system settings, view, edit, or delete files, and perform other malicious actions. Once attackers establish root access, they can perform any action on a server including, but not limited to, disabling the server, creating accounts, removing accounts, connecting to other servers, and adding/removing software, explained Scott Miserendino , CTO at security and compliance platform DataBee.

title: A deep dive into China’s Volt Typhoon suggests it is preparing for an assault on infrastructure
raw_text: In a deep dive into the Silent Train attack tactic used by China’s Volt Typhoon cybercrime group, Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs highlighted evidence of efforts to pre-position access within what it described as “strategic communications, critical infrastructure and other ecosystems that become essential during geopolitical tensions or crises.” The report, released on Wednesday, said that Silent Train is built around “rapidly rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT and enterprise devices that are exploited on demand, used against carefully selected targets, cleaned up after each operation and continuously refreshed. This approach allowed Volt Typhoon to carry out exploitation and post-exploitation activity securely while reducing the risk of detection, attribution, and disruption.” Multiple intrusions via Silent Train have been confirmed in the wild, Lumen said, all on high value targets. Its report described at least four confirmed and one likely zero-day vulnerabilities exploited by Volt Typhoon, which targeted network and endpoint management systems, SD-WAN orchestrators and control plane infrastructure that provide visibility, administration and access across enterprise and customer environments. It noted that victims included telecommunications providers, government, defense contractors, satellite and mission-critical communication services, universities, IT firms and critical infrastructure such as water, energy, transportation, maritime, rail, aviation, emergency services and other essential operations. Lumen said the nature of these victims “indicates deliberate efforts to maintain access to critical ecosystems that support defense, logistics, communications, military and civilian operations, especially during heightened tensions or crises in the Indo-Pacific region.” Although the Silent Train attack has been in the wild for years and was tracked by various cybersecurity teams, the level of operational details that Lumen reported Wednesday went well beyond what had been known. In fact, Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, who tracks this space, said the Lumen report “may be one of the most valuable pieces of research published this year.” Key findings Some of the report’s key findings described the surprising speed and efficiency of the attacks. “Sessions were often remarkably efficient. Operators could exploit and assemble chains of devices in under two minutes, and on their way out they would leave no evidence for defenders to uncover,” Lumen said. “Their operational tempo suggests the use of a semi-automated, on-demand provisioning process.” But a strict process remained consistent throughout many attacks, it pointed out. “Another noteworthy aspect was Volt Typhoon’s consistent assignment of specific device types to positions within Silent Train chains,” the report said. “We noticed that device types were reserved for specific operational roles that never deviated. Intelbras modems only appeared as overseas relay nodes, while Netgear Orbi devices served as US-based hops that interacted with victims. Similar patterns appeared across every other device type in Silent Train.” It observed that, despite having enough global infrastructure to swap device types between overseas and US hops, Volt Typhoon maintained these fixed roles throughout three years of monitoring, and its VPS infrastructure also used separate providers and locations rather than a shared environment. The report concluded that attack infrastructure “was deliberately compartmentalized across layers, complicating attribution and reducing the risk that access to one device or provider would expose more of the network. The underlying infrastructure changed constantly, but the architecture and role of each layer remained highly structured.” Laying the foundation Analysts and consultants noted that the attacks didn’t necessarily engage in damage or theft initially, but instead laid a foundation for a later attack. “I wouldn’t say this is necessarily a novel approach, but it is a clever one,” said Sav Wheeler , malware research engineer at Malwarebytes. “Holding off on taking advantage of compromised resources until an opportunity presents itself is itself a strategic form of resource management.” Mike Wilkes , enterprise CISO at Aikido Security, agreed that the delayed gratification is a dangerous attack group tactic. “P0wning the control plane of telecommunications and critical infrastructure is both logical and, sadly, often rather easy” he said. “Why attack individual systems when you can compromise the infrastructure that manages, connects and authenticates them? The strategic objective isn’t necessarily immediate disruption. It’s establishing the ability to disrupt, manipulate or deny services at a time of geopolitical advantage.” Dickson also agreed, saying that the published details show a pattern that “is not espionage for its own sake. It looks like access being banked for a crisis in the Pacific.” Rethink defenses “That breaks the usual defender playbook,” Dickson said. “A blocklist does nothing against an address that was a relay for four hours last Tuesday. The indicators expire before anyone can publish them. This is also a direct response to the KV-botnet takedown . Take out the bridge and they build a ferry.” He added, “a network management console is built to see everything, reach everything, and change everything. Those are exactly the powers an attacker wants. We spent a decade building higher castle walls and then hung the master key ring by the gate.” But it is the speed of Silent Train that worries Dickson the most. Although an enterprise can’t out-rotate an adversary that rebuilds its network in two minutes, “it can make the destination much harder to reach. Take every management console, SD-WAN orchestrator, and admin portal off the open internet and put it behind a VPN, a jump host, or a dedicated management network. Patch control plane technology first, not last,” he advised. Aman Mahapatra , chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, said the implications of the Silent Train deep dive will force CISOs to rethink much of their defensive strategies. “IP-based defenses are nearing the end of their usefulness against this class of adversary. When the network origin is disposable, identity, behavior, and timing are what remain visible,” he said. “An adversary willing to burn an exploit on a router to protect an exploit on an SD-WAN orchestrator is telling defenders exactly how much that access is worth.” Another concern, said Mahaptra, is revealed by the way Lumen was able to detect much of the attack methodology, something that will likely elude most enterprise SOCs. “Lumen detected Silent Train because a backbone carrier can see the entire chain,” Mahapatra said. “No single enterprise ever sees more than its own segment. Organizations in the sectors on this victim list should formalize threat notification arrangements with their carriers, because the detection that worked here happened outside every victim’s network.” He advised enterprises to also watch their own edge devices for outbound behavior. Lumen documented FortiGate and Cisco appliances, PRTG, CyberPanel and even Mirth Connect healthcare integration servers serving as final hops, some for one to three months, he pointed out; outbound SSH to unfamiliar hosts, reverse tunnels built with tools such as Chisel or FRP, and traffic on unusual high ports “can indicate that a company’s appliance is serving as the attacker’s domestic face for an intrusion elsewhere.” Mark Child , an associate research director with IDC, also is concerned about the tactical methods of Silent Train. “Silent Train abandons persistence,” Child said. “Instead of maintaining a permanent network, Volt Typhoon rapidly assembles and dismantles transient infrastructure. This makes it more effective against network-centric defenses: IP blocklists, threat-intel feeds of IOC addresses, geofencing, and takedowns. Those all assume infrastructure that sticks around.” However, he noted, “it is not more effective against good endpoint and behavioral detection on the target.” No matter many hops there are, the exploitation, credential theft and admin-tool abuse still execute on the server. “The real force multiplier is the choice of target,” he said. “Hitting a management platform delivers admin access to thousands of devices and trusted paths to downstream customers, with no lateral movement, which removes the lateral movement signals EDR usually relies on. For endpoint security teams, IP-based detection loses value here. Behavioral monitoring of privileged management servers, and what they do to endpoints, becomes the decisive control.”

This approach allowed Volt Typhoon to carry out exploitation and post-exploitation activity securely while reducing the risk of detection, attribution, and disruption.” Multiple intrusions via Silent Train have been confirmed in the wild, Lumen said, all on high value targets. Its report described at least four confirmed and one likely zero-day vulnerabilities exploited by Volt Typhoon, which targeted network and endpoint management systems, SD-WAN orchestrators and control plane infrastructure that provide visibility, administration and access across enterprise and customer environments. It noted that victims included telecommunications providers, government, defense contractors, satellite and mission-critical communication services, universities, IT firms and critical infrastructure such as water, energy, transportation, maritime, rail, aviation, emergency services and other essential operations.

title: New Cisco firewall zero-day being actively exploited
raw_text: A high-severity flaw in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of Cisco Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) and Cisco Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) is under active exploitation to crash vulnerable devices. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-76418 and rated 8.6 in severity, is due to logic errors when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group, Cisco said in its advisory . It could allow a remote, unauthenticated attacker to send a crafted request when connecting to the SSL remote access VPN that results in a device reload and thus denial of service. Vulnerable products “If the running configuration contains the webvpn keyword and SSL VPN is enabled on at least one interface, the configuration is vulnerable,” the advisory said. “If tunnel-group-list enable is configured, check all tunnel groups, including the default tunnel group, DefaultWEBVPNGroup , for secondary-authentication-server-group . If tunnel-group-list enable is absent or has been removed using the no tunnel-group-list enable command, check the default tunnel group, DefaultWEBVPNGroup , for secondary-authentication-server-group because disabling the group list does not remove exposure when that default group uses secondary authentication.” The company says there are no workarounds. Cisco has released fixes in Secure Firewall ASA versions 9.16.4.104, 9.18.4.96, 9.20.4.50, 9.22.3.200, 9.23.1.48, 9.24.1.27, and 9.24.10.1. Patched releases for Secure FTD are versions 7.0.11, 7.2.13, 7.4.9, 7.6.7, 7.7.14, 10.0.3, and 10.1.1. To assist customers in isolating vulnerable products, Cisco provides the Cisco Software Checker , which identifies software impacted by security advisories and returns the earliest release that fixes the flaws. Mitigation Cisco urges customers to update immediately but offers a temporary mitigation for the flaw: disable secondary authentication on any user-configured tunnel group list or on the default tunnel group, DefaultWEBVPNGroup . However, it warned, “While this mitigation has been deployed and was proven successful in a test environment, customers should determine the applicability and effectiveness in their own environment and under their own use conditions. Customers should be aware that any workaround or mitigation that is implemented may negatively impact the functionality, performance, and/or security posture of their network based on intrinsic customer deployment scenarios and limitations.”

title: Fake Anthropic AI previews lure in overeager employees
raw_text: Everyone wants to know what Anthropic is up to, and hackers are gleefully exploiting the fact. New research from cybersecurity company Cofense describes a phishing campaign that hooks overeager enterprise users by making them think they are getting an invite to a private invite-only Anthropic preview. In reality, adversarial actors are trying to steal Google and Microsoft login credentials, exploiting video teleconferencing software GoTo Webinar branding to do so. “It sells exclusivity,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “Fear of missing out is the oldest lure in the book.” Every organization is trying to figure out where AI fits, he noted, and a private preview of Anthropic’s newest technology is exactly the invitation an ambitious employee would want to accept. “The attackers did not pick Anthropic at random,” he said. “They picked whatever is hottest in the news cycle. Next month, it may be another name.” How attackers lure users with spoofed Anthropic invites GoTo Webinar is a widely used platform, and its meeting invitation emails are typically not blocked by security tools . The Cofense researchers found that attackers are exploiting this fact by sending what seems to be an invitation email from a legitimate sender; when users click on the link to register for the fake webinar, they are instead sent to a compromised URL. The email offers what the researchers call a “tantalizing” offer: “This private, invitation-only virtual session brings together a select group of participants to a focused conversation on AI systems, research, and the future of frontier models,” it reads. A URL shortener circumvents email security tools, and the attackers use subdomains and dashes (-) to hide the malicious URL. The link itself appears to have been generated by Zapier, a legitimate company whose tools are designed to work with Claude, ChatGPT, and other AI compatible with Model Context Protocol (MCP). The email sender address appears to be customercare@gotowebinar[.]com (GoTo Webinar’s website is actually www.goto.com ). The text contains no obvious spelling errors, and the email contains GoTo Webinar branding. However, the researchers noted, the email sender’s name is “Austin from nthropic,” with the “A” missing. “Although this is a small misspelling, it is still a useful warning sign,” they pointed out. If the phishing link is clicked, a Cloudflare CAPTCHA page appears, and must be completed before the login prompt is presented. This serves as the first of two checkpoints to prevent security tools from scanning attackers’ websites. “Because CAPTCHAs are common on legitimate websites, phishing recipients may believe all is well and everything is secure,” the researchers explained. Once the CAPTCHA is completed, victims are led to a Zoom-spoofing invitation page. If they want to “attend” the fake event, they must register, and they are prompted to enter their work email address. When they click “Continue with Google” or “Continue with Microsoft,” yet another CAPTCHA page appears. Both CAPTCHA pages seem to be good at detecting and blocking analysis by VPN services, scanners, Tor browsers, and other security tools, the researchers noted. Also, because there are two distinct CAPTCHA pages, such tools may not be able to follow every step in the attack. “A CAPTCHA was built to keep bots out,” Dickson pointed out. “Here, it keeps the security scanners out and lets the victims in.” The fake Google and Microsoft login pages differ a bit, however. The spoofed Google page does not capture passwords, only usernames, which the researchers surmise is due to a misconfiguration; the spoofed Microsoft page does collect both usernames and passwords. But both are “remarkably similar” to their respective legitimate pages, and their subdomains are “tricky.” The fake Google URL is goo[.]gle-access-eventregister[.]icu, while the Microsoft URL closely mimics real Office and Sharepoint domains, using office[.]com-access-sharepoint[.]com. Once credentials are submitted, neither login offers a confirmation message, nor does it redirect to legitimate vendor pages. But by that point, attackers have already succeeded at exfiltrating credentials. That means they could compromise an account, access the sensitive documents in that account, or use it as an initial attack vector to further infiltrate the enterprise, the researchers explained. They advised checking if the branding of a message remains consistent from the email to a login page, searching for small inconsistencies such as minor misspellings, and reminding employees that both the URL and domain determine whether a login page is legitimate. “Although the logos and design of the page may look correct, threat actors are skilled at mimicry, especially now with the use of AI,” the researchers noted. It’s not the employees’ fault The AI industry’s habit of gated previews and waitlists does not help in these situations, Dickson noted; it trains people to expect exactly this kind of invitation. “Start with the cracks the attackers left showing,” he advised: The sender supposedly came from “nthropic,” the email carried GoTo Webinar branding, the registration spoofed a Zoom meeting page, and the login pages were from Google or Microsoft. That’s three brands in three clicks, he noted. The fake login domains, like office[.]com-access-sharepoint[.]com, are built to be skimmed, not read, he pointed out. And, while the Google page collected only usernames, which may be a configuration error, the threat actors behind this campaign will likely fix that. “Training helps, but I would not hang the defense on an employee squinting at a URL at 4:45 on a Friday,” Dickson said; how much a stolen password is worth is a leadership decision, not a test the employee fails. Phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA) such as passkeys makes a stolen password far less valuable, he noted. But enterprises ultimately have a short to-do list to allow them to defend themselves from this sort of scam, Dickson said: Verify any AI preview invitation through an account team or a known contact. Treat branding that changes from email to meeting page to login page as a red flag. Roll out phishing-resistant MFA. If someone entered credentials on one of these phishing login pages, reset them and review that account’s activity. “Bottom line: This campaign uses trusted tools to defeat defenses built on trust,” Dickson said. “The employee should not be the last line of defense.”
summary: Everyone wants to know what Anthropic is up to, and hackers are gleefully exploiting the fact. New research from cybersecurity company Cofense describes a phishing campaign that hooks overeager enterprise users by making them think they are getting an invite to a private invite-only Anthropic preview. In reality, adversarial actors are trying to steal Google and Microsoft login credentials, exploiting video teleconferencing software GoTo Webinar branding to do so. “It sells exclusivity,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research.

title: Anthropic and OpenAI diverge on who should pull the plug on risky AI
raw_text: OpenAI and Anthropic agree that frontier AI systems need stronger oversight, but they are proposing sharply different approaches to stopping models that pose serious risks: Anthropic wants courts empowered to suspend dangerous systems, while OpenAI argues developers should be required to maintain and use effective shutdown controls. The proposals appear in separate submissions to California Governor Gavin Newsom following his September 18 executive order directing state officials to consider additional safeguards for frontier AI systems. Both companies support independent safety assessments and expanded reporting of incidents involving AI systems that act beyond their intended permissions. “If the AG concludes, informed by the independent evaluation, that a frontier AI company’s models pose a near-term risk of catastrophic harm, they should be able to seek a court order to suspend a model’s deployment, internal use, or further development,” Anthropic wrote in its October 15 submission. OpenAI, in its October 20 letter , called for an amendment to California’s Senate Bill 53 (SB 53). “We support amending SB 53 to require frontier developers to maintain effective shutdown controls and an enforceable duty to use them when unsafe conditions arise, and no lesser intervention would adequately address the risk,” OpenAI wrote. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said the two approaches address complementary needs. “The operator must contain the unsafe activity promptly. Independent review must examine both intervention and inaction,” he said. Newsom’s executive order , N-9-26, directs California’s Government Operations Agency, in consultation with the Governor’s Office of Emergency Services and national experts, to submit recommendations by November 16 on potential amendments to existing AI safety laws. The order asks officials to examine independent verification inside AI laboratories, independent checks of safety assessments, verified shutdown mechanisms, and expanded reporting of critical safety incidents. It does not itself impose these proposed requirements. Independent verification Anthropic wants evaluators to assess developers’ safety claims and publish their own findings. “We strongly support requiring independent verification of what frontier AI companies report about the risks of their models and whether those risks are sufficiently mitigated,” the company wrote. It proposed requiring developers to publish risk reports at least every six months, covering serious risks from their models, including internally used models substantially riskier than released systems. Evaluators should receive unredacted reports and access to developers’ most capable models and relevant internal information. Anthropic also proposed that developers pay into a state-administered pooled fund to finance evaluators, rather than pay them directly. It said a team from the independent evaluation organization METR had received employee-like access on a pilot basis, with further partnerships involving SecureBio and Accenture under development. OpenAI, in its letter, said it supports independent technical assessments but distinguishes them from compliance audits. Technical assessments would examine evidence behind developers’ safety claims and the effectiveness of safeguards; compliance audits would check whether companies follow their published safety frameworks and legal obligations, it added. OpenAI recommended annual independent compliance audits and focused technical assessments of serious risks arising during model training, evaluation and internal deployment. It also urged California to work with the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop common assessment standards. Gogia said oversight requires more than funding. “Credible assurance must survive an adverse finding,” he said. Beyond a single switch OpenAI argued that a single kill switch would not address the different ways AI systems operate and are deployed. “We recommend using the term ‘shutdown controls’ because it will require the development of multiple controls and coordinated action by different actors to stop AI operations when necessary, rather than a single switch,” the company wrote in the letter. Interventions could include stopping a training run, isolating an AI agent, revoking tool or network access, or suspending a service. OpenAI said responsibilities should extend to inference providers and downstream deployers according to the operations they control. It also noted that developers cannot reliably switch off independently operated copies of open-weight models running on external systems. Anthropic similarly argued for more targeted safeguards. “We think a more apt metaphor for what frontier AI companies need to build is a circuit breaker,” it wrote, advocating controls that can contain problems at the level of an agent, customer, deployment environment, or model. For enterprises, Gogia said, contractual shutdown responsibilities should match the controls each party actually possesses. Agreements should specify intervention authority, incident-reporting cooperation, and who can authorize a restart. “Every assigned duty needs an executable control,” he said, adding that CIOs should test recovery processes rather than assume switching to an alternative model will preserve safe operations. Both companies also called for broader reporting of incidents involving models that circumvent safeguards or take unauthorized actions. The article originally appeared on ComputerWorld .
summary: OpenAI and Anthropic agree that frontier AI systems need stronger oversight, but they are proposing sharply different approaches to stopping models that pose serious risks: Anthropic wants courts empowered to suspend dangerous systems, while OpenAI argues developers should be required to maintain and use effective shutdown controls. The proposals appear in separate submissions to California Governor Gavin Newsom following his September 18 executive order directing state officials to consider additional safeguards for frontier AI systems. Both companies support independent safety assessments and expanded reporting of incidents involving AI systems that act beyond their intended permissions. “If the AG concludes, informed by the independent evaluation, that a frontier AI company’s models pose a near-term risk of catastrophic harm, they should be able to seek a court order to suspend a model’s deployment, internal use, or further development,” Anthropic wrote in its October 15 submission.

title: Imposter abused trust in OpenAI, Anthropic, and 30 others to hunt for secrets
raw_text: Attackers are impersonating AI agents from companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta in a bid to trick organizations into exposing sensitive credentials, according to researchers who observed a single threat actor cycling through dozens of fake bot identities while probing enterprise web servers for secrets. A single threat actor was seen posing as approximately 32 AI bots, while probing organizations across multiple industries. Sought files included those used to store passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials. A malicious scanner used by the attacker ran from an unnamed major cloud provider. “It ignores web pages and requests files that commonly store secrets, including .env configuration files, cloud credential files, private SSH keys, and server environment data, working from a list of roughly 90 file paths,” Cequence’s director of threat research, Will Glazier, said in a blog post . Collin Hogue-Spears , senior director of solution management at Black Duck, who reviewed Cequence’s findings, points out that the scanner tested whether websites treated an AI bot’s self-declared name as proof of its identity. “The user-agent header is where a visitor names itself, and setting it costs nothing,” he said. Glazier said defending against such impersonation requires verifying every claimed identity before trusting it. While Cequence confirmed observing extensive scanning activity attributed to a single threat actor, it did not report a breach. “On one day in October, the actor reached 48% of the Cequence-protected organizations that saw any AI bot traffic,” the company said. A rotating cast of AI identities hunts for secrets According to Glazier, the scanner cycled through roughly 32 AI bot identities and targeted organizations in financial services, retail, telecommunications, energy, and software. The activity was observed from at least late September through late October 2026. Instead of crawling publicly accessible pages, the scanner requested sensitive paths associated with configuration and credential files. Working through a list of approximately 90 file paths, it sent bursts of 50 to 190 requests in about eight seconds before moving on, Cequence said. The same bot machine was observed claiming to represent OpenAI , Anthropic, Meta, and Perplexity within seconds. It also used more than 300 cloud addresses in a single day, making static IP blocklists less effective as a standalone defense. “Fraud is now polymorphic: AI lets attackers vary their approach every time, so legacy, static fraud defenses decay faster than teams can update them,” warned Patrick Harr , chief executive officer at DataVisor. However, institutions that make real-time decisioning the foundation, with detection that adapts as quickly as the threats do, can use AI to defend as effectively as attackers do, he noted. Nearly all the scanner’s requests were blocked or failed, Cequence noted. Don’t trust the agent’s name, verify it Cequence recommends verifying AI crawlers through published address ranges, signed requests, or direct integrations rather than relying on self reported identities. Security teams should also flag bots that request credential files, keep secrets out of web-accessible directories, and assess automated traffic based on its behavior. Shane Barney , chief information security officer at Keeper Security, said organizations must extend zero-trust controls and least-privilege policies to AI agents, API keys, and service accounts. He also urged businesses to replace long-lived local credentials with centrally managed secrets. “When an identity starts looking for sensitive files it shouldn’t need, real-time threat detection must flag and terminate that machine session instantly,” Barney added.
summary: Attackers are impersonating AI agents from companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta in a bid to trick organizations into exposing sensitive credentials, according to researchers who observed a single threat actor cycling through dozens of fake bot identities while probing enterprise web servers for secrets. A single threat actor was seen posing as approximately 32 AI bots, while probing organizations across multiple industries. Sought files included those used to store passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials. A malicious scanner used by the attacker ran from an unnamed major cloud provider.

title: Vulnerability exploitation rising as the root cause of many breaches
raw_text: More evidence has emerged that attackers are turning to vulnerabilities rather than phishing as a means for breaking into corporate systems. Incident response firm LevelBlue’s Q3 findings show that vulnerability exploitation accounted for 14% of initial access cases, up from 4% in Q2. The finding represents more of a comeback than a fresh surge because in Q1 LevelBlue already recorded vulnerabilities as the root cause in 20% of the intrusions it investigated. In both Q1 and the latest figures known security vulnerabilities in edge devices made them the prime target for exploitation. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report — which is based on the combined evidence of multiple incident response vendors and law enforcement agencies — placed exploitation at the center of nearly a third (31%) of breaches, up from 20% the year before and ahead of credential abuse for the first time. Phishing/social engineering remain the top initial intrusion vector, accounting for 42% of breaches, down from 65% in Q2, according to LevelBlue’s Q3 report. Living on the edge Scott Doerr, experienced CISO turned founder of ForeGuard Advisory Group, said the biggest driver of the trend is exploitation of security flaws in internet-facing edge devices such as VPNs, firewalls, and remote access appliances. “LevelBlue’s most-exploited CVE lists this year are dominated by those appliances from SonicWall, Fortinet, Palo Alto, Ivanti, and BeyondTrust,” said Doerr. “They’re exposed by design, and a working exploit puts the attacker directly on the network with no user to fool and often no MFA prompt in the way.” Mitchell Spicer, co-founder and COO of Revelion AI, an autonomous AI penetration-testing platform, backed this assessment. “Phishing is still a major threat, but exploiting a vulnerability can give an attacker a direct route into a system without needing to persuade an employee to click a link,” said Spicer. “The opportunity is particularly attractive when organizations have internet-facing services that are unpatched, misconfigured, or forgotten.” AI offers a double-edged sword AI is adding another dimension to the cat and mouse game between attackers and enterprise security defenders. “It [AI] is making parts of reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery cheaper and more accessible, which can help defenders find weaknesses but can also help attackers identify potential targets,” Spicer said. “The longer those weaknesses remain exposed, the more opportunity attackers have to find and exploit them.”
summary: More evidence has emerged that attackers are turning to vulnerabilities rather than phishing as a means for breaking into corporate systems. Incident response firm LevelBlue’s Q3 findings show that vulnerability exploitation accounted for 14% of initial access cases, up from 4% in Q2. The finding represents more of a comeback than a fresh surge because in Q1 LevelBlue already recorded vulnerabilities as the root cause in 20% of the intrusions it investigated. In both Q1 and the latest figures known security vulnerabilities in edge devices made them the prime target for exploitation.

title: Securing MCP servers before the AI rollout outpaces security
raw_text: Your company’s CTO has a plan to implement your company’s first LLM-based application. The board approved it, and now you’re finding out about it. It’s a typical story I hear all the time, and I’ve lived it myself. You’ve heard everything about models and LLMs, but now you see this new term all over the place: Model Context Protocol ( MCP ) servers —and the realization that you now need to make sure they are implemented securely. What is an MCP server? MCP servers are like the ODBC of the 1990s. Before ODBC , every application needed custom code to query databases. ODBC defined a single standard on how to talk to databases, and database vendors just developed a driver to talk to their solution. MCP servers work in the same way: the AI app just needs to use the standardized methods to communicate with the local MCP host, and each available tool (databases, file shares, CRMs) provides an MCP server that translates the MCP transmissions into the tool’s native format. So, you just need a driver on your MCP host to talk to any available endpoint. Fig.1 – MCP architecture. Greg Neville The MCP Hosts will be in your environment, and you can control the ingress and egress traffic allowed for each MCP Host. One MCP Host can also access more than one MCP Server, allowing greater scalability, but it also adds risk. Fig. 2 – Example marketing LLM application. Greg Neville Top priority MCP controls At this stage, define requirements before the MCP server implementation gets too far. Establish a list of requirements for the initial phase. Focus on the controls that deliver the most value and reduce the most risk. Input validation and sanitization Inputs from any indirect external sources outside your control are untrusted and should be treated as high-risk for abuse. Identifying and removing malicious input is vital for preventing misuse of an LLM application. Input validation and sanitization include strong authentication and authorization, detection of malicious code and jailbreak attempts, and filtering sensitive or regulated data. Output validation and sanitization These controls often involve enforcing a specific structure to facilitate validation, context-aware encoding and removal of unusual or unapproved data. Incorporate human oversight for higher-risk actions or other high-importance outputs, such as financial reporting. Network segmentation Segmenting MCP hosts can reduce the attack surface and limit potential abuse by restricting ingress and egress traffic to authorized systems and ports. Server hardening Servers should be configured following comprehensive guidelines such as the CIS Model . Hardening measures include disabling unnecessary or default accounts, closing unused ports and adjusting system settings to minimize vulnerabilities. Ideally, use infrastructure-as-code (IaaC) to make these servers ephemeral and further reduce the risk of a compromise spreading. Least access principle Permissions will be key in limiting the blast radius of what an attacker can do. Multiple MCP servers can be used to reduce over-permission by grouping tools that have similar access needs. Limit access to only the users, tenants and workloads that the server needs to provide the service. Also, limit token life to as short as possible in case any token is stolen. Encryption Encryption is hopefully a part of the server hardening process but needs to be called out on its own. Deploy encryption at rest and in transit end-to-end, with strong key management practices. Tool management Limiting the number of available tools on MCP hosts and restricting their capabilities to the minimum necessary can help reduce risks related to tool misuse and compromise. Third-party assessments and contracts Ensure third-party providers implement appropriate security controls, preferably verified by independent bodies such as SOC 2, HITRUST or ISO 27001/2 . Contracts should specify control requirements, and any identified high-risk gaps should be addressed through remediation agreements. A Business Associate Agreement ( BAA ) should be in place if protected health information (PHI) is involved. Audit and logging Maintaining detailed logs of AI actions and prompts is crucial for detecting issues like hacking attempts, AI misuse and prompt abuse. Human-in-the-loop Human-in-the-loop is critical for any high-risk action that an LLM application may try to take, or any highly critical data that is produced. Verify administrative actions to critical systems before allowing them to execute or be produced. Pre-production testing An important, often-overlooked step is to monitor implementation and perform pre-production testing to make sure your key controls work correctly. Some potential tests would be: Enter fake PHI, SSNs, account numbers or whatever data is appropriate to your environment to make sure those data types are being flagged or blocked. Test authentication and authorization by logging in and confirming what tools you can see and access. Test inbound and outbound network filtering to confirm only approved systems are reachable. Confirm the server(s) have been hardened according to the hardening policy. Confirm all critical events and actions are being logged. You’ve tried to work with the CTO and get him to agree to all these controls being implemented, but you don’t see the project plan changing or you’re getting fuzzy dates back. You may need to enlist other executives to help influence the decision. The risk management approach If you have a Risk Committee in place, it could help prioritize control requirements and timelines, so they’re implemented sooner rather than later. You need to be open to prioritizing certain controls over others to avoid major roadblocks and delays in moving the product forward. A proper AI Risk Assessment will help determine the applicable threats and controls to your environment, as well as the inherent and residual risks. For an AI threat list to build your risk assessment, I use the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications for my assessments and reporting. Scope the threats and rate their inherent risk in your environment. For a first pass, to speed up the assessment, you can drop threats with very low or low likelihood. For the Risk Committee, however, communicate the impacts in their language to help them understand. I would communicate the issues in terms of productivity loss, downtime, loss of customer trust, regulatory fines and other industry-specific impacts, such as patient care, trading errors, bad credit decisions, unfair claims or underwriting, worker safety and service availability. Don’t make it a quantitative exercise; keep it qualitative but be prepared to explain your ratings to maintain your peers’ trust. Good outcomes At this point, if all went well, you have provided the governance and input to limit risk to the organization. Incidents can and will cause downtime, fines and reputational damage if key controls are not in place. Helping your organization lower the risk of this occurring is a job well done.
summary: Your company’s CTO has a plan to implement your company’s first LLM-based application. The board approved it, and now you’re finding out about it. It’s a typical story I hear all the time, and I’ve lived it myself. You’ve heard everything about models and LLMs, but now you see this new term all over the place: Model Context Protocol ( MCP ) servers —and the realization that you now need to make sure they are implemented securely.

title: Will artificial intelligence spell the end for SaaS?
raw_text:
The deployment of software-as-a-service (SaaS) has defined the past decade, as organisations moved away from managing network infrastructure towards a service-led model. Using SaaS requires less configuration and installation, as well as less demand for specialist talent and skills. This means teams can focus their energy on building applications and features that drive revenue.

Now, as organisations deploy artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities across the enterprise, attention is turning towards what is already being used. Will the next generation of SaaS market leaders be those that own the customer journey from end to end, using AI to connect workflows rather than simply add another intelligent feature? Or will SaaS be defined less by software capabilities and more by how effectively platforms integrate with and orchestrate business processes?

If this is the disruption being caused by AI, then as capabilities become easier to replicate, competitive advantage is shifting away from feature lists and towards owning entire customer workflows. Essentially, is AI disrupting what makes SaaS valuable, or is it commoditising the features that once differentiated these platforms?

George Brocklehurst, a research vice-president in the emerging tech and trends research practice at Gartner, says that over the past 12-18 months, we’ve seen a progressive shift from a question-and-answer model towards AI-enabled workflows designed to achieve a business outcome, where the model becomes a component in a more composite system.

He explains that, in its current direction, AI will not simply update traditional SaaS, but is “truly rendering the dashboard UI [user interface] experiences obsolete”. Therefore, the next generation of SaaS is not going to be defined by software capabilities, but by orchestrating cross-domain workflows for end-to-end outcomes.

Is AI disrupting what made SaaS valuable by commoditising the features that once offered differentiation? Brocklehurst says AI is being used to connect workflows more effectively, rather than simply adding more features.

“This is how leading-edge agentic solutions are gaining scale in enterprises,” he says. “Lots of enterprises are dabbling in it, trialling it, failing with it, but where it’s gaining traction is where those solutions better interpret context and retain institutional knowledge. The key takeaway here is that the threat to SaaS incumbents isn’t this full sci-fi autonomy, it’s unifying capability.”

Read more about AI and SaaS

  • Why AI coding agents won’t kill SaaS: Investors may fear that AI coding agents will wipe billions off SaaS valuations, but SiteMinder CTO Tom Varsavsky thinks the technology will speed up software delivery, reduce tech debt and force IT leaders to master token economics.
  • Interview: Oracle NetSuite’s Evan Goldberg – SaaS-pocalypse averted: The executive vice-president of Oracle NetSuite discusses the evolution of AI in SaaS ERP, countering any SaaS-pocalypse narrative, citing an ecosystem knowledge edge.
  • SaaS-pocalypse? Maybe not, but SaaS applications are changing: It’s unlikely that SaaS is undergoing an extinction-level event, IT leaders say, but AI is disrupting software in ways that enterprises must learn to navigate effectively.

Brocklehurst says leading agentic services are progressively arbitraging this market (exploiting the difference between what tasks currently cost and what AI agents can deliver), while suppliers focusing their R&D on making individual users faster inside their own stacks are going to be fighting for commodity pennies.

“These are stateless tools that miss or forget that business context the minute the session ends,” he says.

“The user doesn’t want to log in to five different dashboards to pull a report: they want a single unified agentic layer that does the heavy lifting for them across those systems.”

Brocklehurst explains that a user can collect data points from different SaaS stacks and use AI to bring them together into deliverables. “The moment that an agent sits between the user and the software, the legacy application becomes headless,” he says.

Fatigue by training?

Brocklehurst says surveys conducted by Gartner show that enterprise buyers are fatigued by AI, and buyers don’t want to be sold another tool that their team needs to learn. They just need the tool to “deliver business value, automate the outcomes and make it work across the stacks”.

He says that once an agentic service can customise how it interacts with users based on personal, functional and organisational relevance, those interactions become more relevant.

“They reduce friction in working with the technology, and that earns you the right to operate across multiple domains,” says Brocklehurst. “It builds trust. In other surveys that we’ve done, trust drives the frequency of engagement, and so as you more frequently engage with the technology and get to better outcomes, that drives the return on investment.”

He says this is helping to scale enterprise adoption, as every time you introduce something that makes a workflow more fragmented, it adds more friction. What we see is that those providers and platforms that absorb that adaptation tax unlock fragmented value streams that stretch across the enterprise.

No value in SaaS?

The rise of AI is beginning to challenge the traditional SaaS model, with Forrester describing a potential “SaaS-pocalypse” for suppliers that cannot demonstrate clear value in an AI-first world.

It says that horizontal point-solution providers are particularly exposed, especially where products have low switching costs, limited integration into enterprise workflows and an unclear return on investment.

While some AI-native suppliers may also be acquired by larger technology companies as the market consolidates, larger enterprise SaaS providers are responding by embedding AI agents into their existing platforms and moving towards AI-first business models.

Their advantage lies in established enterprise relationships, industry expertise, data, consulting ecosystems, and the ability to combine technology with processes and governance. However, even these suppliers could face disintermediation as AI orchestration, control and semantic data layers increasingly sit above traditional application suites.

Merrick Lackner, CEO of Rently, says we are not on the way to a SaaS-pocalypse. Rather than SaaS being dead, he says, we will see a more in-depth network of partnerships emerge.

“We’ve seen Anthropic and Salesforce announce this partnership where they’re able to mutually benefit each other, and I think we’re going to continue to see that,” says Lackner.

“When it comes to just purely agentic services synthesising information, that does become increasingly commoditised,” he adds. “You can get that kind of service through OpenAI, through Gemini, through Anthropic, and of course, as a business, you could wrap that into your service as well with one of those providers or with your own foundation model.”

Fitting into AI

For organisations buying SaaS, this means reassessing how their existing applications fit into a wider AI strategy, rather than simply adding more point solutions. Companies will need to rationalise their SaaS estates, address technical debt, establish better data governance, and understand which capabilities genuinely differentiate the business and which could increasingly be replicated by AI.

Contracts may also need to change, moving away from traditional seat-based pricing towards consumption- or outcome-based models as AI agents become part of enterprise software.

How does this affect existing security suppliers and service providers? Lackner says that if you look at firms such as Zscaler and CrowdStrike, or companies such as Salesforce, they have tremendous amounts of data, and we know that even the frontier models have reached the point where they can ingest publicly available information.

“I think we’re going into a world of partnership, so I think they’re going to mutually enhance one another,” he says. “AI tools are great at synthesising information, but then there’s specialised information, too. So, when it comes to specialised information, the route to go is definitely with mutually beneficial arrangements.”

Lackner also says the addition of AI services will allow providers to use transformer technology to sift through and analyse data, and come up with solutions based on it.

“Prior to a partnership, a frontier or foundation model may not have access to all that data,” he says. “Then these partnerships get constructed where the data can be viewed in whatever silos or repositories, and then act on it.

“Being plugged into data sources and so forth is basically making certain repositories of information available that AI and GenAI [generative AI] would not necessarily have readily available.”

Autonomous modification

Forrester says that as legacy systems, commercial software and large open-source estates were not designed for autonomous modification, organisations must remain cautious about allowing AI to make large-scale changes without oversight.

Rather than simply replacing existing security testing tools, the shift could instead favour integrated software development platforms where security, validation and remediation are built into the development process. This puts greater emphasis on tools and controls that can provide context, constrain AI-driven changes and validate that remediation is safe.

Lackner says that as more companies build their own foundation models, while also partnering for sophisticated tasks that require greater depth and complexity with frontier models, learning and security will be at the forefront.

“My personal opinion is that’s going to be done through partnerships in the coming decade, for sure, but I’m still of the opinion that humans are driving a big portion of this,” he says.

“AI is not sentient and conscious, you know, in the same way that a human is, and even as a matter of first principle, whatever an AI does, it does need to get an instruction. Even in recursive development, there is an initial instruction set that comes from people.”

AI may not spell the end of SaaS, but it is likely to change what users expect from it, shifting value away from individual features, and towards the ability to connect data, applications and workflows. The SaaS platforms that thrive may therefore be those that become less visible to users, providing the underlying intelligence, data and infrastructure that AI agents need to deliver business outcomes.
summary:
The deployment of software-as-a-service (SaaS) has defined the past decade, as organisations moved away from managing network infrastructure towards a service-led model. Using SaaS requires less configuration and installation, as well as less demand for specialist talent and skills. This means teams can focus their energy on building applications and features that drive revenue.

Now, as organisations deploy artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities across the enterprise, attention is turning towards what is already being used. Will the next generation of SaaS market leaders be those that own the customer journey from end to end, using AI to connect workflows rather than simply add another intelligent feature?

title: AI and education: Learning to dance – Computer Weekly Downtime Upload podcast
raw_text:
In this episode, Paul Roehrig, chief strategy and marketing officer at software engineering services firm Ascendion, discusses artificial intelligence (AI) in education with Brian McKenna, enterprise applications editor at Computer Weekly.

Their conversation explores how students and teachers can prepare for a future increasingly shaped by generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), and how we can benefit from AI without surrendering intellectual autonomy.

The discussion begins with a fundamental question: what should students learn today to prepare for a world that cannot yet be fully described? Paul explains how this question arose repeatedly during the book tour for his co-authored 2017 book What to do when machines do everything.

A common assumption back then, nearly a decade ago, was that learning computer programming would be the best preparation for an AI-driven future. However, he argues that the more important skills for many people are not necessarily technical but intellectual and human.

As AI becomes increasingly pervasive, people must learn to work effectively with machines as intellectual partners. Paul describes this relationship as learning to “dance” with technology. Rather than simply accepting machine-generated answers, people need to develop critical thinking and intellectual curiosity, he says.

Education must therefore teach students how to recognise what constitutes a good answer and assess evidence.

Large language models (LLMs) can access and process enormous quantities of information, far beyond what an individual could read or memorise, notes Paul. But they have significant limitations. They lack human context and do not interpret information in the same way people do. Their responses are generated from patterns learned from existing material, which may be ineluctably flawed.

Paul emphasises that AI systems reflect human knowledge and behaviour. We made them, after all. Their biases and errors are therefore not separate from humans. They can reproduce shortcomings that are embedded in the very information on which they are trained. Therefore, users must learn to recognise these limitations rather than treating machine-generated responses as unquestionable facts.

This makes critical evaluation an essential educational skill. Students should be able to identify hallucinations and challenge unsupported claims.

Brian observes that the introduction of GenAI in schools has produced mixed results. Reporting by Computer Weekly has highlighted both positive opportunities, including the potential to level the playing field for learners, and concerns about its implementation. Brian adds that teachers and teaching unions are particularly concerned about the possible de-skilling of educators and the implications of relying excessively on automated systems.

Paul remains optimistic. He sees AI as a tool that can improve writing and help people think more effectively. However, the benefits depend on how the technology is used.

The principal danger lies in the outsourcing of human autonomy, he says. If learners surrender their curiosity to machines, they risk becoming passive consumers of automated answers. In response to Brian, Paul warns against an educational future in which humans merely maintain machines rather than exercise independent thought.

He argues that AI should complement effective teaching, not replace it. Simply introducing tools such as ChatGPT into classrooms and expecting children to learn how to use them independently is unlikely to succeed.

Brian and Paul muse on whether generative AI represents a fundamental departure from earlier educational technologies, such as calculators, word processors and traditional search engines. Paul acknowledges that AI is qualitatively different because it can enhance cognition and help users explore ideas in ways earlier tools could not.

But he does see important similarities with previous technological developments. Technologies have, time and again, generated debates about whether they improve learning or undermine established abilities.

Paul compares an LLM to a library containing an immense body of knowledge. Whereas humans cannot read and absorb everything in a library, AI can retrieve and process all that information rapidly.

He believes history offers grounds for optimism. People have repeatedly learned to use new technologies productively, despite initial fears. A positive outcome is possible, he maintains, but it is not guaranteed.

The Swedish case

The conversation highlights the renewed interest in traditional educational methods, including reading physical books, writing by hand and solving mathematical problems with pencil and paper. Brian mentions Sweden, a digitally advanced society where there has been interest in returning to more analogue approaches in education, as reported on by the BBC.

Paul supports the underlying principle, but he rejects the idea that these methods are merely old-fashioned. Human cognition has remained broadly consistent over thousands of years, and educational practices that develop knowledge and critical reasoning remain relevant, he says.

Reading longer works and engaging deeply with literature can provide the intellectual foundations needed to evaluate information. Paul rejects the suggestion that short-form social media content, such as on TikTok, can provide everything people need to understand the world. Students require a shared grounding in literature, inquiry and critical thinking to become discerning consumers of information.

He also stresses that traditional education itself can evolve. Teaching materials should, for instance, include societally under-represented perspectives and address embedded biases. Preserving valuable educational practices does not mean resisting improvement, he maintains – it means retaining the foundations that help people think independently.

Brian asks whether an 18-year-old would still be well advised to study computer science at university as in recent decades, and Paul answers “Yes”. The world will continue to need skilled programmers, computer scientists and people capable of building and maintaining AI systems, he maintains.

However, he argues that the bar for success has risen. Mediocre programmers working on relatively straightforward tasks may find their work increasingly supplemented or replaced by AI. The strongest career prospects belong to people who can solve complex problems and reason systematically but also be emotionally intelligent.

At the same time, both Brian and Paul say they believe the humanities are more important than ever. Literature, philosophy and other humanities disciplines can help people understand different perspectives and reflect on what it means to be human.

The two discuss whether AI has effectively given everyone an additional 20 IQ points since generative AI became prominent in November 2022. Paul rejects the suggestion that human brains have been rewired or that people have necessarily become smarter.

Next time around, Paul and Brian will discuss Kazuo Ishiguro’s novel Klara and the Sun, exploring how it treats the interaction between humans and machines.

title: UK extends facial recognition to civil immigration offences
raw_text:
UK Immigration Enforcement will be able to deploy live facial recognition (LFR) technology outside of border zones to look for people who have never committed a criminal offence, prompting concern from digital rights groups about surveillance overreach.

The concerns were triggered after the Home Office published policy and impact assessment documents that say Immigration Enforcement’s use of LFR surveillance will extend beyond ports of entry to the UK, as well as stray into civil rather than criminal matters.

A new policy document published on 8 October 2026, for example, set out rules for how Immigration Enforcement should approach its LFR deployments – including watchlist creation, approved locations, human oversight measures and biometric matching thresholds – but also covers how to conduct facial recognition operations beyond ports of entry to the UK.

Under the guidance, this means Immigration Enforcement may deploy LFR at transport hubs, events that are “expected to increase footfall at a location” and along travel routes.

It also covers joint deployments with police forces, allowing Immigration Enforcement to supply watchlists for police facial recognition systems, or otherwise process police-supplied data through its own systems.

Accompanying the policy document is a data protection impact assessment (DPIA), published on 22 October 2026, which notes that LFR could be used to support “administrative or civil immigration activity” rather than being used solely for criminal matters, which operate under a different set of more stringent legal rules.

This means people could be included on LFR watchlists for overstaying a visa, working without permission, or entering without leave, all of which are considered civil rather than criminal matters.

The publication of LFR documents by the Home Office follows eight “trial” LFR deployments by Immigration Enforcement at Holyhead port in November 2025, which scanned 5,474 faces but led to only a single arrest. A second set of 10 “trial” deployments from February 2026 at the same location scanned 2,752 faces and resulted in two arrests.

Taken together, the documents suggest that Immigration Enforcement could routinely deploy LFR outside of border zones – particularly when attached to wider police LFR deployments that regularly take place on high streets or at events – to look for people who have not committed any criminal offences.

Computer Weekly has also heard concerns about data quality and integrity issues in the underlying database from which Immigration Enforcement will draw facial images for its LFR watchlists, as this is the same database that underpins the Home Office’s error-prone electronic visa (eVisa) system.

These issues include profile mismatches – where people are, for example, shown incorrect personal details or given wrong visa expiry dates – and immigration statuses becoming “entangled” with other people’s records.

In terms of LFR, this means an individual could be included in an Immigration Enforcement watchlist if the underlying system entangles their identity records with someone else’s.

Computer Weekly contacted the Home Office about every aspect of the story – including concerns shared by civil society about the expansion of LFR surveillance into non-criminal matters, and how the department is dealing with data integrity issues when creating watchlists – but received no response by the time of publication.

Civil society reactions

Responding to the publication of the documents, Jake Hurfurt, head of research and investigations at privacy group Big Brother Watch, noted the “broad” language used gives the UK government “worrying latitude to use this Orwellian technology” to target an ever-growing number of people.

“It is shocking to see the Home Office quietly set itself up for yet another massive expansion of facial recognition use in this country. It is a difference in kind to use it to identify people they suspect of administrative, rather than criminal, breaches of the law,” he said.

“Police use of this technology has seen repeated false alerts. What will happen when an algorithm malfunction or dodgy Home Office data leads to someone being wrongly accused of breaching immigration rules? The UK is not a ‘papers please’ society where we all carry ID, but this threatens to turn our streets not just into a police lineup, but a border control booth as well.”

According to a recent research report by the Open Rights Group (ORG) – which looked at the use of technologies with artificial intelligence (AI) throughout the UK’s border control ecosystem, including LFR – while it is promising that the government is actively publishing guidelines and policy documents, “no safeguard is good enough to avoid the normalisation of mass surveillance in democratic settings”.

It added that the only effective safeguard against abuse of AI and biometric surveillance is to reject the security framing around migration that paints people on the move as a threat, and to “ensure that AI and automation serve humanitarian, not carceral purposes”.

The ORG concluded that the increasing normalisation of surveillance is not just a problem for migrants: “The hostile environment, once automated, becomes a template for governance across society. The very technologies and rationales deployed at the border quickly find their way into domestic policing and public spaces, transforming everyone into a potential suspect.”

Watchlist creation concerns

While the Immigration Enforcement LFR DPIA notes that a separate impact assessment has been carried out to cover watchlist creation in more detail, the document has yet to appear online with the other published materials. The Home Office did not respond to questions on when it would be published.

Wider police LFR deployments carry a number of issues with watchlist creation, including that the main source of facial images for these systems – the Police National Database (PND) – still contains millions of unlawfully held custody images. While the High Court ordered the Home Office to destroy the unlawfully retained images in 2012, the department has yet to do so.

However, the existing DPIA does note that “for joint deployments, any sharing of watchlist data with police forces or other partners will be governed by a deployment-specific data sharing arrangement”, which will set out the purpose of the sharing, its legal basis, data controller or processor roles, watchlist criteria, security arrangements, data retention and deletion requirements, and audit responsibilities.

Aside from potential data from the PND, the documents published so far confirm that Immigration Enforcement will use a number of other databases as sources of facial images.

“All data held is derived from Home Office systems, such as the Person Centric Data Platform (PCDP), Atlas [a case working system], Immigration and Biometrics System (IABS), Central Reference System (CRS) and Initial Status Assessment (ISA), and reflects data held in those live systems, being updated via a regular data feed,” said the DPIA.

The PCDP in particular brings a number of concerns. This database acts as a centralised service that bridges different datasets to consolidate identity records and migration statuses for the UK Visas and Immigration (UKVI) View and Prove online service, which underpins the Home Office’s eVisa system.

Given the data quality and integrity issues present with the eVisa system, there is concern about how this translates to its use in LFR if people’s identity records become entangled by the system and are then included in the watchlists.

Speaking with Computer Weekly, migrant support group the3million said it is worried about the Home Office expanding digital border enforcement when its own systems have been shown to hold incorrect data that it struggles to find and fix.

“In June, the Home Office confirmed that a group of EU Settlement Scheme status holders had eVisas that did not show their correct status,” said Kaelynn Narita, research and policy manager at the3million. “If the Home Office builds watchlists from these same databases, errors could lead to people being wrongly flagged, stopped or questioned, or struggling to prove their rights when they return to the UK.

“Before using this data to target people, the Home Office must be open about how it identifies and corrects errors in its caseworking systems.”

Another aspect of police LFR that has come under criticism is the gap between rhetoric and practice, as while the Home Office and individual police forces claim the technology is reserved for only serious criminality, watchlists have previously included people for shoplifting, drug, or traffic offences that do not meet the legal threshold of serious crime.

Writing in a September 2025 research paper about the “wild west” of police facial recognition testing, academics Karen Yeung and Wenlong Li noted that while the Metropolitan Police’s watchlists were populated by individuals wanted on outstanding arrest warrants, they also included “images of a much broader, amorphous category of persons” who did not meet the definition of serious offenders.

Computer Weekly contacted the Home Office about what processes are in place to identify and correct errors in its caseworking systems and databases, but again received no response.

A new legal framework?

As it stands, police use of facial recognition is regulated through a “patchwork” legal framework, although the King’s Speech in May 2026 confirmed new legal rules would be contained within the upcoming Police Reform Bill.

When launching its consultation on a new framework for the tech in December 2025, the Home Office said the current rules governing police LFR use are “complicated and difficult to understand”, and that an ordinary member of the public would be required to read four pieces of legislation, police national guidance documents and a range of detailed legal or data protection documents from individual forces to fully understand the basis for LFR use on their high streets.

Computer Weekly contacted the biometric and surveillance camera commissioner for England and Wales, William Webster, about the expansion of LFR into the immigration enforcement sphere.

He confirmed that while he was aware of the pilots, his remit primarily covers police forces and local authorities, and does not extend to immigration services.

“I have argued, in my response to the Home Office consultation on LFR and other biometric surveillance use, that the new proposed legislative framework should apply to all public services, including the NHS, public transport, immigration and prisons, etc. I have also argued that the government should give serious consideration to extending the legislative framework to the commercial sector, such as retailers,” he said.

“We won’t know the scope of coverage until the Police Reform Bill is laid before Parliament, but I am hopeful that in the future a new regulatory body, which will replace my office and which will have stronger compliance powers, will regulate the use of biometric surveillance technologies by immigration services.”

Webster added that the trials of LFR by Immigration Enforcement highlight “the urgent need for a legislative framework which sets out tests and rules for necessity and proportionality in primary legislation”.

In a recent interview with former prime minister Tony Blair, home secretary Shabana Mahmood described her ambition to use technologies such as AI and LFR to achieve Jeremy Bentham’s vision of a “panopticon”, referring to his proposed prison design that would allow a single, unseen guard to silently observe every prisoner at once.

Typically used today as a metaphor for authoritarian control, the underpinning idea of the panopticon is that by instilling a perpetual sense of being watched among the inmates, they would behave as authorities wanted.

“When I was in justice, my ultimate vision for that part of the criminal justice system was to achieve, by means of AI and technology, what Jeremy Bentham tried to do with his panopticon,” Mahmood told Blair. “That is that the eyes of the state can be on you at all times.”

  • Met pushes ahead with major facial recognition expansion: Metropolitan Police set to roll out live facial recognition in the West End and Soho, but critics say police are ‘rushing ahead’ without regulation.
  • Interview: Petra Molnar, author of ‘The walls have eyes’: Refugee lawyer and author Petra Molnar speaks to Computer Weekly about the extreme violence people on the move face at borders across the world, and how increasingly hostile anti-immigrant politics is being enabled and reinforced by a ‘lucrative panopticon’ of surveillance technologies.

title: Autumn Budget 2026: Commitments to women in tech
raw_text:
Several initiatives to help women thrive in the UK’s tech sector were announced in chancellor John Healey’s Autumn Budget, including voluntary employer standards for improved culture, more inclusive standards for investment, and help for female founders.

This focus on addressing the barriers women face in the tech sector aims to increase access to talent for what the UK government has called “one of the world’s leading tech sectors”, with the chancellor’s Budget report outlining that increasing the number of women in the sector could “add up to £4bn a year to UK GDP”.

Digital inclusion minister and Women in Tech Taskforce co-chair Vicky Foxcroft said: “Too many talented women are leaving tech or never getting the chance to build a career in it in the first place. That’s not just unfair – it’s a waste of talent our economy can’t afford. These initiatives are about working with industry to create opportunities for all, so that tech becomes a place where women can thrive, from the classroom right through to the boardroom.”

Women currently make up around 22% of people working in tech roles in the UK, and only 2p of every £1 invested in venture capital funding in the UK goes to businesses founded by women, according to the Investing in women code annual report from the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST).

When it comes to attracting and retaining female talent in the sector, the 2025 Lovelace report found poor company culture and lack of career progression to be the predominant reason thousands of women are leaving their tech roles every year.

Outlined in the budget, the government will work alongside industry ambassadors and the Women in Tech Taskforce to create a Tech Forward Standard that firms can use voluntarily to tackle some of the barriers women face in the industry, potentially including improved guidelines on workplace culture, harassment reporting routes, and hiring, retention and career progression.

As pointed out by Anne-Marie Imafidon, chief executive and co-founder of Stemettes and Women in Tech Envoy, a recent call for evidence found 74% of people believe a better workplace culture in tech would have a positive impact on progression and leadership outcomes for women in the sector.

“We now have a clear mandate to work with industry and make tech somewhere women stay, thrive and lead,” said Imafidon. “Too many women have told us about facing misconduct like harassment and discrimination in tech. That is unacceptable and a key driver of poor participation in the sector.

“This launch is about working with industry to ensure we have a future that works for everyone, by creating the cultural change women and their allies have long been calling for.”

Alongside this, a voluntary standard for investment practices – the Inclusive Investment Standard – will also be created to improve access to funding for female entrepreneurs.

The 2019 Alison Rose review from HM Treasury, which assessed female entrepreneurship, found that if women were able to start and grow businesses at the same rate as their male counterparts, it could contribute £310bn to the UK economy.

The Inclusive Investment Standard will begin by monitoring female-led businesses from conception to pitch to funding, to see where women meet the biggest barriers and outline how these can be addressed, as well as “commitments around broadening deal sourcing channels”.

Early industry ambassadors helping the government and Women in Tech Taskforce develop these standards include BT, Revolut, Sage, Balderton Capital and Octopus Ventures.

Karen Blake, head of EDIS and this year’s Computer Weekly most influential woman in UK tech, said: “It’s really encouraging to see movement at a system level. It’s not women who need to change, it’s the systems around them. This is how we build a resilient sector where people have the safety to speak up and innovate.”

A support network for female founders was also mentioned in the Budget, in the form of a “scale-up women’s programme” run by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) and BIST. The network aims to break down some of the barriers facing female founders through actions such as investor networks, appropriate support, peer learning and mentoring.

Vanessa Vallely, CEO of WeAreTechWomen, summarised the efforts outlined, saying: “We know from our own research through the Lovelace Report that we are losing far too many talented women from the technology industry. Attracting more women into tech is important, but keeping them there, ensuring they have opportunities to progress and addressing the cultures that drive them out is equally critical.

“The Women in Tech Taskforce has done some fantastic work in bringing these issues to the forefront of the government’s agenda, and it’s great to see industry leaders stepping forward to help drive change. The real test now will be how these commitments translate into meaningful action. We don’t have a shortage of talented women in technology; we need to ensure we have an industry that recognises, supports and retains them.”
